en: When a cognition is to be produced,
[the object] must be the qualifier of a cognition whose substantive is that which is produced by that sense-faculty and possesses a non-conceptual (laukika) contact with that same sense-faculty.

The meaning is that the "universal" (sāmānya) constitutes the sense-object contact. Regarding the phrase "and of being produced by the mind": although the universal of cognition as a whole is indeed produced by the mind—since it exists in the presentation of atoms—it is nevertheless [stated] because even recollection is produced by a sense organ by way of being a temporal condition (kālopādhi).

To prevent that [undesired consequence], one must intend to specify only that "producedness" (janyatā) which is delimited by a property (upādhi) that is a differentiator of perception and is itself defined by the generative capacity (janakatā) residing in that sense-faculty;

since such producedness by the mind exists only in the cognition of pleasure and so forth, there is no inconsistency. Regarding the term "bhūmikām," it refers precisely to the reasoning (yukti) conducive to the introduction [of the subject].
Regarding the phrase "the generality that is being known" (*jñāyamānasāmānya*):

if the category of "generality" (*sāmānyapadārtha*) were restricted to the [eternal] genus (*jāti*) alone, then since an impermanent generality (*anityasāmānya*) would be unestablished, it would be impossible to point out a fault against such a view.

Therefore, in order to avoid that [consequence], it is pointless to abandon the category of "generality" and instead accept that the cognition of it constitutes a means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Thus, [the author speaks of] the impermanent...
It should be understood that the establishment of the status of being a *sāmānya* (universal) is intended as a means for introducing the subsequent portion of the text.

Regarding the phrase "of those that are similar" (*samānānām*) in the root text: the point is that, in this context, the word *sāmānya* is etymological (*yaugika*) rather than technical (*pāribhāṣika*). Regarding the term "inclusion" (*parigraha*): although [it occurs] by way of inherence (*samavāya*),...
Since the locus of that jar is indeed the potsherd itself, the phrase "of the potsherds and so forth" (*kapālādīnām*) in the root text is inconsistent; nevertheless,
because the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the preceding sentence includes cloth and other such things as well, in accordance with that, [the commentary states] "where there is one jar."

There is no inconsistency [in the argument], because the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) in the preceding sentence also functions as an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) for cloth and so forth; thus, by means of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of threads and other such materials is possible.

By the phrase "time and so forth" (*kālādi*), there is the inclusion of cognitions and the like which possess the property of being "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) through the relation of being the object (*viṣayitā*); this is because they are to be brought forward later by the very reasoning stated immediately prior.
However, the phrase "but this is inconsistent" (kiṃtu ityasaṃgatam) indicates that its meaning is as follows: "and thus [the meaning is] 'in this way'.

For although in the perceptual cognition "this pot-possessing potsherd," one might suppose that even the property of being a pot (ghaṭatva) is a qualifier (prakāratā) with respect to the potsherd by means of a mediated relation (*paramparā-sambandha*) immediately after the destruction of that [pot], [the following applies].
This is because there exists the very perception of the skull and so forth which serves as the basis for that [inference]. Nor should it be asked:

"What is the recourse even in such cases of verbal cognition and the like? For in those instances as well, by way of the requirement of a qualified-qualificand relation (*viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya-bodha*), the pot is related to the possessive suffix-meaning (*matubartha*) through the relation of being determined (*nirūpitatva*), just as in the previous case.
Because it is possible for "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva), which has attained the status of a qualifier of that [substance], to also be connected [with the cognition],

and because even in the cases of inherence (samavāya) and conjunction (saṃyoga), the relation of being the substratum of the substratum (svāśrayāśrayatva) can be conveyed by the possessive suffix -matup; thus, wherever there is a verbal or other type of knowledge in the form "this possesses that individual," [the suffix conveys the relation].

The inconsistency should be understood as arising from the impossibility of "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) being a qualifier in any way whatsoever. As for the question, "Why is it not produced?": here, although if the cognition "this is a pot" on the following day were of the nature of recollection or the like, there would be no such contingency precisely because it would not be produced by that sense organ; however, if it is visual (cākṣuṣa), [the problem remains].

In that case, since the necessity of visual contact [with the object] exists, there is no possibility of such an objection; nevertheless, the objection should be understood by taking into account extraordinary (alaukika) visual perception. "By intending the state of being a qualifier" means by way of excluding that which possesses a qualificandum-ness co-temporal with its own qualificandum-ness. Otherwise, [the following would occur].

The point is this: when there is visual contact with smoke, even though there is a non-ordinary visual perception (*alaukikacākṣuṣa*) of the form "the pot at the time of the smoke" based on the recollection of smoke, this perception would then—by means of the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) of "smokeness"—result in a visual perception of all smoke by the eye. [Objection: But surely [it is] "possessing that pot"?

Alternatively, in the view that generalization (sāmānyapratyāsatti) is the means of perception, although the fact that the cognition "this is a pot-fragment" has "potness" as its qualifier with respect to the fragment-part is not established by perception, it must be inferred there for the sake of subsequent effects; this is the underlying intention [of the author].
He states the cumbersome complexity resulting from the inclusion of "belonging to that person" (tatpuruṣīyatva) with the words "In this way.

[This refers to] by means of a proximity residing in the person (*puruṣaniṣṭhapratyāsatti*). [The phrase] "connected with the sense organ by inherence" (*samavāyena indriyasaṃbaddha*) is used. Now, one might object:
even if, under this alternative view, the mere cognition of a universal (*sāmānyajñāna*) constitutes the proximity, there is no fault.

With the intention that the production of knowledge through the proximity of the universal (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*) during a state when there is no connection with the sense organs must be prevented by the author himself, he says "or else" (*yadvā*). He demonstrates another advantage of brevity (*lāghava*) in this alternative view, saying "and thus" (*tathāca*), and "and by the postulation" (*kalpanena ca*). By the word "and" (*ca*):

There is a compounding of the heaviness of the body of the delimiting condition (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) due to its inclusion of the qualificandum known through the previously shown qualifiers. Although,
in place of "having a universal as its mode" (*sāmānyaprakārakatva*), one might introduce "having a universal as its object" (*sāmānyaviṣayakatva*).

Even on the view that [the cause] is the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) of cognition, it remains as before; nevertheless, this mention is intended to show that the delimiting condition of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) consists of a triad—this is how it should be understood.
"Commonality with indeterminate perception and recollection" means being of the nature of indeterminate perception and so forth, which are included within cognition.

And this [term] "mere general cognition" (*sāmānyajñānamātra*) is intended here in the sense of the generality of general cognitions (*sāmānyajñānasāmānya*). According to this author's view, he demonstrates the relationship between the property that delimits the effect and the property that delimits the cause by saying "and thus" (*tathāca*). In the case of perception produced by the general character (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*), there is necessarily [the presence of] potness (*ghaṭatva*).

The inclusion of "having potness as its qualifier" (*ghaṭatvaprakārakatva*) is for the purpose of accounting for its appearance as a qualifier by making it a constituent of the delimitor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*). Even so, one might object: since in perception an object cannot appear without sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*), and since there is no general relation (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*) with respect to potness, how can potness [appear]?

It must be stated that [the object] appears in a perception produced by a general cognition (*sāmānyajñāna*) such as recollection (*smaraṇa*), because the cognitive proximity (*jñānapratyāsatti*) exists therein. Regarding the phrase "having become its own qualifier" (*svaprakārībhūta*):
this is merely prima facie; for if that were the case, [the problem would persist] in a perception produced by the general-characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of potness and so forth.

For otherwise, the restriction that all jars and so forth are perceived would be untenable. Rather, it should be understood that the relation which delimits the effect-status (kāryatāvacchedaka-sambandha) is precisely the non-ordinary objectivity (alaukika-viṣayatā); and in the case of a jar that is in close proximity, two types of objectivity are admitted because of the presence of the causal factor (prayojaka). Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: "But..."

In the view that universal-cognition (*sāmānyajñāna*) constitutes a means of immediate perception (*pratyāsatti*), although there is simplicity (*lāghava*) in the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) according to the previously mentioned method, [the causal relation] is between a non-sensuous perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*)— which has as its qualifier a property (*dharmaprakāraka*) produced by a specific sense-organ (*tadindriyajanya*)— and a perceptual cognition produced by that same sense-organ (*tadindriyajanya*) through the universal-characteristic means of immediate perception (*sāmānyalakṣaṇapratyāsatti*).

Since it must be postulated that a heavy causal complex composed of various factors possesses the status of a cooperative cause for that [perception], and since in this system it is necessary to postulate the causality of a much heavier complex for a perception produced by a general relation (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*) due to the difference in sense organs, this is not [the case] in this view.

There is even talk of parsimony (lāghava). Nor should it be argued that, according to the ancient view, an infinite number of cause-and-effect relations must be postulated due to the difference between persons, whereas in the new view there is no such requirement, and thus parsimony exists; for even in this [new] view, the causal complex (sāmagrī) is composed of the visual contact belonging to that specific person and so forth.

Since it is necessary to postulate that, according to worldly relations, the causal capacity for a visual perception belonging to a particular person resides in the causal complex consisting of the contact of that person's eye and so forth— by means of those same relations— there is no such parsimony [in the opponent's view]; otherwise, [the perception] would arise from a causal complex consisting of the contact of another person's eye and so forth.

He dispels the doubt—that there would arise for another person, even one with eyes closed, a visual perception produced by the general proximity [of the object] despite possessing only a general cognition—by describing his underlying intention, stating:
"This is the intention. He explains: "The causal complex for visual perception, etc. This means the causal complex for a qualified visual perception, and so forth.

It should be understood that by this [means], even non-conceptual [perception] is attained; otherwise, a specific visual perception such as "this is a jar" in the subsequent moment would be untenable. This is because of the acceptance [of this principle];
that is, because such an acceptance is possible. And this [is stated] in the absence of evidence [to the contrary].
Since it has been established that the causal complex (sāmagrī) delimited by the pervading property (vyāpakadharma) is the productive cause, for that very reason,

one cannot infer the occurrence of a visual perception of "pot-ness" and so forth— produced by the person's own general cognitive proximity (sāmānyapratyāsatti)— in a situation where the causal complex consisting of the visual contact of that person and other factors is absent.

In the view of the Navya school, since there is no need to postulate an additional causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), the economy of theory (*lāghava*) remains entirely intact. Regarding the phrase "if [it] consists of cognition" (*jñānarūpā yadi*), it is not possible for the word "if" (*yadi*) to connect with what precedes it, because the nature of being cognition (*jñānarūpatā*) is the definition of cognition itself (*jñānalakṣaṇā*).

Since this is established by all disputants, he says "pertaining to this" (*atratya*) in order to ward off confusion regarding that. Because what is about to be stated does not constitute the meaning of the text to be explained, he says "this is the intended meaning" (*ayam abhiprāya*).
"Due to the absence of contact" (*saṃnikarṣābhāvāt*) means due to the absence of contact qualified by [the object's] being situated within the range of perception (*yogyavṛttitva*).

Therefore, there is no inconsistency; for even though the relation of inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) is necessary for the fragrance at the time of the eye's contact with the sandalwood, there is no harm [to our position]. Alternatively, this response is intended with reference to an erroneous perception (*bhramātmakapratyakṣa*), such as "the sandalwood is fragrant," and thus there is no lack of coherence.

[The author] refutes the objection that—in the perception "this is fragrant sandalwood"—the manifestation of fragrance is possible through the very means of knowledge known as *sāmānyalakṣaṇa-pratyāsatti*, which consists of a cognition having "fragrance-ness" (*saurabhatva*) as its qualifier—by stating "saurabhatve... [and so on]. Now, in the root text:

The objection beginning with "even if" (*yadyapi*) and so forth is not tenable, because—as stated previously—it is impossible for there to be a possessor of fragrance (*saurabhavān*) through a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*); therefore, he states its existence with the words "fragrant" (*surabhi*) and so forth. And in this context, the reading *saurabhatvāvacchinnaprakāraka* is a corrupt one.

If the proximity consisting in the character of being an object of knowledge (*jñānalakṣaṇapratyāsatti*) is not accepted, it would be impossible to establish the causal complex for the perception in question as having "fragrance" (*saurabha*) as its qualifier; rather, the reading must be "perception having 'fragrance-ness' (*saurabhatva*) as its qualifier.
This is because, with such a reading, there exists the non-sensory (*alaukika-mānasa*) causal complex for the perception having "fragrance-ness" as its qualifier.
It should be understood that this is because there is no possibility of its arising [through other means]. Regarding the phrase "by way of its own nature" (*svarūpataḥ*):

although it is possible for that [fragrance] to be manifested through the universal characteristic of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) and so forth, the manifestation of its specific nature as "the state of being fragrant" (*saurabhatva*) would not be possible if the "characteristic of knowledge" (*jñānalakṣaṇā*) were not admitted.

[This refers to] the state of being [an object]. It should be understood that in the phrase "dharmāntara" (another property), the word *antara* (other) has entered [the compound] by way of accidental occurrence (*saṃpātāyāta*), because in the aspect of "saurabhatva" (the nature of fragrance), nothing appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*). [The phrase] "due to the impossibility of its manifestation" refers to the general cognitive proximity (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*) consisting of the knowledge of "saurabhatva."

Even if the relation of extra-sensory objectivity (alaukika-viṣayatā) as determined by the mode-ness of "fragrance-ness" (saurabhatva-prakāratā) were the delimitor of the effect (kāryatāvacchedaka-sambandha), [the cognition would still not arise] because of the rule that in perception only that which is in contact [with the sense organ] appears, and thus there is no generalization (sāmānyalakṣaṇā) regarding fragrance-ness.
The meaning is that [the cause] is absent due to the relation that delimits its causal status (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka-sambandha*).

One must accept that the cognition of "saurabha-ness" (fragrant odor-ness) and so forth has causal efficacy only with respect to perception as delimited by "perceptuality" (*pratyakṣatva*) through the relation of extra-sensory objecthood (*alaukika-viṣayatā*). As for the appearance of "saurabha-ness" and so forth as a qualifier (*prakāratā*), however...

In a perception produced by generalization (sāmānyapratyāsatti), it is indeed accepted that there is the manifestation of another uncontradicted property (dharmāntara) even when it is presented solely through the force of another cause consisting of the cognition of a qualifier; furthermore, the restrictive rule that "in perception, that which is not the locus of the sense-contact is not manifested" is not admitted at all in the case of visual perception of a jar and the like.

With the intention that the non-appearance of cloth and so forth is possible precisely due to the absence of the causes for its appearance, he says: "the delimiting factor of being an effect. This means a relationship of that kind. Regarding the phrase "qualified perceptual cognition": [it is] with respect to a perception having that as its qualifier, by virtue of being a cognition of that [qualifier].

The intention is that this is stated with the sense of [establishing] causality; thus, because the causal relations are distinct due to the difference in the properties that delimit the effecthood (*kāryatāvacchedaka-dharma*), it is impossible for one to be otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*) by the other—this is the point.
Now, an objection: in perception, the proximity of cognition (*jñāna-pratyāsatti*) should not be accepted as a cause.
Since the reasoning regarding the causality of the cognition of a qualifier has already been demonstrated previously, he says:
"Thus, where... [and] "having its own object as the primary qualificandum.

And so, with respect to a perceptual cognition of a worldly type (*laukika-pratyakṣa*) having that [object] as its content, [the cause is] by virtue of being a cognition having that [object] as its content.

The sense is that causality is necessary; otherwise, since there would be a non-ordinary (alaukika) manifestation of time with respect to a particular such as a jar, it would follow that the manifestation of the jar itself becomes non-ordinary. "Therefore he says" means that with this intention, he states the purpose of the cognitive proximity known as *jñānalakṣaṇapratyāsatti*.

Thus, may there be auspiciousness. 65. Thus ends the first wave, on perception, in the *Dinakarīya-taraṅgiṇī*. "And here is the connection" (*saṃgatiśca atra*): the meaning is that the connection for the definition of inference follows immediately after the definition of perception. The sense of the locative case is "being the motivator" (*prayojakatva*), [which resides] in the referent of the word "connection."
Its connection (*anvaya*) is to be understood as follows:

*Asaṅgati* (inconsistency) residing in the object to be defined is the relationship conducive to the recollection of that which is the object of a cognition which generates the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) that serves as the motivator for the immediate subsequent statement. To explain: * **Connection (*anvaya*):** This refers to the logical relation between the preceding and the subsequent. * **Inconsistency (*asaṅgati*):** This is the specific type of relationship existing in the subject matter (*nirūpaṇīya*) that prompts the reader to wonder why it is being discussed immediately after the previous topic. It is a relationship that facilitates the recollection of the subject matter of the preceding cognition, which in turn gives rise to the curiosity necessary to justify the transition to the next point. Thus, it is as follows: [the text continues].

Following the definition of perception, the motivating inquiry regarding the definition of inference takes the form, "May I possess inferential knowledge. The cognition that produces this [inquiry] takes the form, "Inferential knowledge is the means to achieve my desired end. The object of that [cognition] is inference.

*Saṃgati* (logical connection) is a relationship conducive to the recollection [of a previous topic], specifically the state of being an effect of perception established through inference. Here, the cognition that serves as the motivator for the subsequent mention [of a topic] should be qualified by its being produced by the cognition that defines the *saṃgati*. By this—

Even after the determination of a jar or similar object, although there is the possibility of inference and recollection as effects of that [perception] within a perceptual cognition dependent on the knowledge of a specific relation, there is no contingency of the status of being a concomitant (saṅgatatva) being attributed to the jar and so forth merely because they are effects of perception. This is because [the case of] inferential cognition...

Because it is not caused by the cognition of a jar. And in the present case, since inference—in the form of the cognition of pervasion—is produced by the eye and other [senses], the sense is that inference possesses the status of being dependent (*upajīvaka*) insofar as its effect is the product of the means of valid cognition known as perception (*pratyakṣa*). The same applies to inferential cognition (*anumiti*) as well.

It should be understood that because inferential knowledge (*anumiti*) is produced by a perceptual valid cognition (*pratyakṣapramiti*) whose nature is reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), the definition of inference follows immediately after the definition of perception. Now, the offering of a lamp ought to be a means for my eyesight,
since the Veda declares that "the lamp is the supreme eye" as a means for vision.

[Objection: Since there is activity toward the offering of a lamp based on the inference "because it has been awakened," and since the manifestation of the visual faculty (*cakṣus*) and so forth produced thereby depends upon that inference, why is perception (*pratyakṣa*) not defined immediately after the definition of inference? And it is not the case that...

It should not be argued that "the state of being dependent (upajīvakatva) consists solely in the form of being an effect (kāryatā) and not in the form of being prompted (prayojyatā); therefore, since the eyes and other senses do not directly possess the quality of being produced by inference, there is no contingency of defining perception immediately after defining inference. For if that were the case, [the following would follow].
Since comparison, which consists of the knowledge of the capacity [of a word], is useful only for the recollection of the object,
it does not directly produce verbal cognition; therefore, it is logically untenable to define verbal cognition immediately after comparison.
Nor should it be argued that being a dependent (upajīvakatva) without the mediation of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is the regulator for the immediate mention [of a subsequent item];

for in a case where one proceeds toward a mirror and such by means of an inference of its being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), there occurs the destruction of the great eye by means of that mirror.

It is also possible that there exists a dependence upon [the sense of] sight— specifically a particular instance of the visual organ— without the mediation of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit). Furthermore, if it is argued that there is no dependence upon inference with respect to the delimiting property of being a means of valid perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇatva*),
because the mind and the ear are not produced [by anything else], and because all inference whatsoever [is dependent on perception]...
If it is considered that there is no possibility of establishing a contrary conclusion because [the cognition] is produced by the mind, the form, and the sense organ,
then even the Lord's knowledge of pervasion would be an inferential indicator (anumāpaka) by virtue of its being capable of taking the form of an inference.

If it is argued that, because inference lacks the quality of being a subordinate consequence (*upajīvaka*) of perception, the determination of inference immediately after perception is likewise untenable— this is not so.
For there is no rule that whatever is logically connected must necessarily be determined immediately thereafter.

By this [reasoning], the definition of perception follows immediately after the definition of inference. However, there is an invariable concomitance (vyāpti) such that whatever is defined immediately after something else is connected to it;
for as the learned say: "One should not employ what is disconnected. And thus, whether in the case of a cause or an effect...
When something is known, the desire to investigate whether it is an effect or a cause arises;

thus, both being dependent (*upajīvakatva*) and being that upon which another depends (*upajīvyatva*) constitute *saṃgati* (logical connection). For this very reason, even the exposition of inference immediately following the exposition of inferential cognition in the *Cintāmaṇi* is consistent. Nor is it the case that...

If both the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and the state of being a cause (*kāraṇatva*) were considered types of connection (*saṃgati*), the sixfold nature of connection would be contradicted; as it has been said: "The sixfold [connection] consists of: introduction (*saṃprasaṅga*), digression (*upoddhāta*), causality (*hetutā*), occasion (*avasara*), unification of the supporting factor (*nirvāhakaikya*), and unification of the effect (*kāryaikya*)."
It should be stated that "conjunction (saṃgati) is desired [as the definition]. This is because conjunction, by way of the relations of being a determiner (nirūpakatā) and being a locus (āśrayatā),
is included within the very nature of causality (hetutā), since the property of being an effect (kāryatva) is nothing other than the state of being a determiner of causality.

Because it has the nature of being an effect (*kāryatā*). In that context, *prasaṅga* (relevance) is a relationship that serves as the cause for recollection, distinct from *upoddhāta* (introduction) and other such categories.
*Upoddhāta* consists in being a support for the subject at hand (*prakṛtopapādakatva*). Nor does this [function] by way of being a reason (*hetu*) consisting of causality.
The sense [of the passage] is already understood;

for, through the introductory connection (*upoddhātasaṃgati*) to the definition of inference, the fact that a qualified reflective awareness (*viśiṣṭaparāmarśa*) is the cause of inference has been established. Indeed, in the definition, what is meant by "the state of being a cause" (*hetutva*) is not the state of being a cause either directly or indirectly; rather, it is—
It should be understood that [the term] refers exclusively to that which establishes [a subsequent topic]. "Occasion" (avasara) means the state of being due to be discussed immediately after;
for example, when, following the definition of perception, both inference and comparison—being its effects—are reached as the proper subjects for definition.

It should be understood that since the desire to know arises first regarding inference itself—due to its being accepted by many disputants—the determination of comparison (*upamāna*) follows the determination of inference; this is based on the "connection of occasion" (*avasara-saṅgati*), which occurs when the obstructing desire to know has been removed by the determination of inference.
"Unity of the sustaining factor" (*nirvāhakaikya*) means being produced by the same motivating cause. "Unity of the effect" (*kāryaikya*)...

"Conduciveness to a single effect"—this is the direction [of the argument]. "By way of being related" means by way of being related through pervasion (*vyāpti*). Regarding the phrase "the qualifier in the qualificand":
this refers to the cognition "smoke is pervaded by fire" when it involves the apprehension of the qualified as possessing the qualifier (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyāvagāhitva*).
The sense is that [inferential cognition] is impossible without a verbal reflective awareness (*śābdaparāmarśa*). Regarding the phrase "by way of parsimony" (*lāghavena*):

in order to exclude inference from a reflective awareness that takes the form of a doubt regarding the element of pervasion—such as "the mountain possesses smoke which either has pervasion or lacks it"—one must [require] a certainty regarding the element of pervasion, just as one does regarding the element of smoke.
It would be cumbersome to require that [the cognition] be a certainty (*niścayatva*).
However, when a cognition apprehending a qualified-qualificand relation (*viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya-avagāhi-jñāna*) is taken as the cause,

[the objection is avoided] because the [required] certainty is already precluded by the very fact that it constitutes the cause— the certainty regarding the qualifier delimited by the delimitor of the qualification (*kāraṇībhūta-viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka-prakāraka-niścaya*).
The sense is that there is no purpose in including [the condition of being produced by the same cognition] because doubt regarding the element of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is impossible.
"By means of the relation of a mental impression" (*saṃskārasambandhena*) means "by means of the relation of a mental impression produced by itself.

[This refers to] the consideration (*parāmarśa*) of the knowledge of pervasion through either the relation of inherence in the mental impression produced by itself or [the relation of being produced by itself].

The sense is that because it is a cause, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) anywhere. Regarding the phrase "by way of being the pervader of the reflective awareness" (parāmarśa): one should understand that the reflective awareness possesses the state of being the pervaded (vyāpyatva) through identity (tādātmya). [The opponent claims] that causality itself does not exist; for when there is the presence of a property that pervades the delimiting factor of necessary antecedence (niyatapūrvavartitāvacchedaka), [the effect follows] by means of the pervading property (vyāpakadharma).

The meaning is that [the reason] is otherwise established in its capacity as a cause. "Mere reflection" (paramarśamātra) means mere cognition; the sense is that the root *mṛś* preceded by *parā* has the meaning of "cognition.
Regarding "the mark" (liṅga): the mark is a reason characterized by both pervasion and the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

The meaning is that it should be understood that the cause of inference is precisely the cognition qualified by that [object] through the relation of objectivity (*viṣayatā*). It must be considered. Now, one might object that in this way, deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is unavoidable in the case of an inference produced by another [inference];
in response to such a doubt, he says: "and the delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*)," and "both the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the subject (*pakṣa*).

Although it is difficult to state a single definition of "certainty" (*niścayatva*) common to both, provided that it consists in not having the absence of that [object] as its qualifier (*tadabhāvāprakārakatve*).

Since the nature of certainty (*niścayatva*), which consists in having that [property] as its qualifier (*tatprakārakatva*), is constituted by specific properties such as the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the subject (*pakṣa*) which have become qualifiers,
[there is no certainty] in the nature of certainty consisting in having that as its qualifier.
Because it is constituted by specific properties of the subject (pakṣa) which serve as the pervaded (vyāpya) and the qualifier (prakāra),

and because there is no commonality among the relations that delimit those qualificative states (prakāratāvacchedaka-sambandha), if the relational objectivity (sāṃsargika-viṣayatā) were not specified individually [with respect to each relation], then [cognition] would [occur] through temporal and other such relations.

Even if one were to grant that inferential cognition (*anumiti*) would arise from the consideration of the pervaded (*vyāpyaparāmarśa*), it would be difficult to establish a single, uniform nature as the cause; nevertheless, [the required state] is that which is characterized by the subjectness (*pakṣatā*)— which has as its counter-positive a relation delimited by the delimitor of the cause (*hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha*) and delimited by the delimitor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), and which is further related to the mode (*prakāratva*) through a relation delimited by the property of being a locus (*ādheyatva*).

That which is a subjectness delimited by pervasion, not delimited by any relation other than the delimiting relation of the reason (hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha), and which is qualified by a qualifierhood that is not itself qualified by the absence of the pervaded (vyāpyābhāva)—

wherein that qualifierhood is delimited by the delimiting relation of the reason and is not qualified by a modehood (prakāratva) of the absence of the pervaded where such modehood is delimited by a relation other than the delimiting relation of the reason, and [furthermore] is not delimited by any relation other than the relation of being located (ādheyatva) as delimited by the delimiting relation of the reason.

The intention is as follows: it is possible for there to be a unified causal status based on the nature of a cognition possessing a subjecthood delimited by the delimitor of the pakṣa (the subject of inference), because according to the established doctrine, the property of being delimited by a relation resides only in the modehood (*prakāratā*) and not in the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*). Even so, [this applies] by way of the absence whose counter-correlate is the pervader (*vyāpaka*).

Furthermore, it is simply impossible— whether one posits the absence of the object of negation (*abhāva*) or the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) in general— to include within the definition a certainty (*niścaya*) regarding smoke in a place lacking light, or to exclude the doubt (*saṃśaya*) as to whether or not there is smoke that is not a pervader of fire, even when considering cognitions of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*).

With the intention that, because absences must be included within the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the cause for the determination of each individual among those of diverse forms, a common causal nature is likewise impossible, he presents another view, beginning with "of the two kinds" (*dvividhayoḥ*). [He says] "by way of that form" (*tādrūpyeṇa*).
"By having the subject as the qualificand" means by having the pervaded (the middle term) as the qualificand.

He sets forth his own view with the words "in reality, however. [The phrase] "in accordance with experience" means that inference arises only from a *parāmarśa* (reflective awareness) that has the subject as its qualificand, and not otherwise.

The meaning is that this is because it conforms to the experience that inferential cognition (*anumiti*) has the pervaded (*vyāpya*) as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*). The meaning is that [the suffix] *śānac* is prescribed by the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau* as a substitute for the present tense (*laṭ*) when it has the sense of the present time; this is the intention.

Although it is thus inconsistent to posit two causalities, nevertheless,

The point is that there is no inconsistency [in the objection], because the intention is to show that, according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, there is no complexity (*gaurava*) since the relationship of cause and effect is established as being heavy (i.e., fundamental). It should be understood that there is complexity (gaurava) because, in the case of inclusion (niveśa), an infinite number of cause-and-effect relations would result due to the difference in the delimiters of pervasion (vyāpyatāvacchedaka). According to the view of Bhaṭṭācārya, however, it should be stated [that the inferential cognition] possesses a subject-predicate relation (viśeṣyatā) regarding the pakṣa, which is itself determined by a predicate-relation (prakāratā) delimited by a subject-predicate relation (viśeṣyatā) that is determined by a mode-of-apprehension (prakāratā) of pervasion (vyāpti).

Because the relationship of the delimited and the delimiter (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*) is accepted between the modehood (*prakāratā*) and the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in a single locus,

if one were to accept the identity between qualificandhood and modehood, it would follow that the cognition "the man with the red staff" (*raktadaṇḍavān*) would be contradicted by a certainty regarding the absence of the staff having the red color as its qualificandum (*raktarūpaviśeṣyaka-daṇḍābhāvaniścaya*).

It should be noted that such a cognition possesses a qualificand-ness residing in a red color, which is itself determined by a mode-ness of the staff. He says "knowledge of complexity" because the determination of causality does not depend on the complexity that is about to be mentioned. [He says] "by another means of knowledge."

The meaning is: a means of valid cognition other than inference based on an effect as a logical mark (*kāryaliṅgaka-anumāna*). "Having its own locus" (*svāśrayakatva*) means existing in its own locus. "Dependent upon certainty" (*niścayādhīna*) means that [the establishment of the probandum] occurs only when there is certainty regarding such a causal capacity (*kāraṇatā*), by means of the mark of the effect.

The meaning is that it is possible for there to be a determination (*nirṇaya*) of the *parāmarśa* qualified by its occurrence immediately prior to the inference. "Being a constituent part of itself" means being a constituent part of the complexity (*gaurava*). "Not such [a thing]" refers to a cognition of complexity that arises subsequent to itself.
The sense is that there is no possibility of [the opponent's argument] being an obstacle. Regarding the term *upoddhāta* (introduction):

since the cognition that apprehends the qualification of both the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and the subject (*pakṣa*) is produced by the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the definition of *parāmarśa* (reflective awareness) follows immediately after [the discussion of pervasion] by way of this introductory connection (*upoddhātasaṅgati*).

The meaning is "the determination of pervasion" (vyāptinirūpaṇam). Regarding "being a constituent" (ghaṭakatvam): it is the state of being that which is not the object of a cognition whose object is not itself;

If the possession of the probandum (*sādhyavatva*) by means of the delimiting relation of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) is not intended [in the definition],

To address the objection that [the definition] is non-existent on a mountain and so forth, he states the meaning of that text: "by whatever [connection]" (*yenakenacit*).

[This is] the state of being. It should be understood that the statement regarding "non-pervasion" (avyāpti) is made because the definition is possible in cases such as "that which possesses a nature qualified by being different from what is not produced by fire" or "that which possesses that [fire's] nature due to its taste. If it is considered that there is no over-extension because the activity of atoms produced at the time of dissolution— which is not simultaneous with smoke— is precisely what is meant here, since its occurrence [in the subject] via the delimiting relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is unestablished, then it is with that very intention that the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is used.

Furthermore, it is impossible to exclude the difference from the smoke of the kitchen (*mahānasīya-vahni-mad-bheda*).

Moreover, it should be noted that even if the delimitation of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) is not established for a heavy property (*gurudharma*)—on the view that a heavy property cannot serve as a delimitor when the delimitation is pervasively distributed (*paryāpta*) over the property qualified by the counter-correlativity—this does not cause any deficiency in the argument. Thus...

It should be understood that even the root phrase "unrestricted by the property of being the absence of occurrence in what is other than the locus of the probandum" (sādhyavadanyāvṛttitvatvāvacchinna) means "having a delimitor that is pervasively distributed over [the property of] such occurrence. Otherwise, it would be impossible to exclude the absence of occurrence in the lake *Mahā-hrada* (which is not a locus of fire). In this way, [the definition of the fallacy of] "occurrence in what is other than the locus of the probandum" (sādhyavadanyavṛttitva) [is established].
It is precisely the state of being the counter-positive of the relation delimiting the probans-ness, as qualified by having for its relatum something other than that which possesses the probandum;

it is not, however, the state of being located (ādheyatva) in that [locus] as delimited by that relation and as determined by something other than that which possesses the probandum, because such [locatedness] is unestablished when the probans-ness is defined by a relation that does not regulate occurrence (vṛttyaniyāmaka-sambandha). That which is not the deliminator of such locatedness...

It should be understood that even in the phrase "the delimitor of the causal state" (*hetutāvacchedaka*), the meaning is precisely "that which is not the delimitor of such a counter-correlativity" (*tādṛśapratiyogitānavacchedaka*).

Regarding the phrase "of the qualified inherence" (*viśiṣṭādheyatāyāḥ*): although it might be argued that this is simply because the qualified is not distinct [from the constituents], [the author] says...

That must be stated, and it has indeed already been stated in the root text; nevertheless, even though the qualified entity is not distinct [from its constituents], the locus-of-beingness (*ādheyatā*) residing in the qualified is distinct. Thus, although the locus-of-beingness delimited by pure existence (*śuddhasattā*) is determined by qualities and so forth, the locus-of-beingness delimited by the qualified is not [determined by them].

It should be understood that this was stated precisely to dispel the doubt as to whether [the property] is defined by qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the state of being purely positive" (*kevalānvayitve*):

it refers to the time of the ascertainment of pure positivity, which consists in the state of not being a delimiting factor (*anavacchedaka*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of difference.

This is the meaning. "Containing the constituent of pakṣatā" (*pakṣatāghaṭaka*) is a corrupt reading; for doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhyasaṃdeha*) alone constitutes *pakṣatā*, and since *pakṣatā* in the form of the absence of proof (*siddhyabhāva*) does not consist of doubt.
Rather, the correct reading is "consisting of *pakṣatā*" (*pakṣatātmaka*). Thus, [the question is]: "Is it denotable (*vācya*) or not?"

The sense is that there is no inference precisely because doubt is absent. In reality, according to the established doctrine (siddhānta), it is accepted that "subjectness" (pakṣatā) consists solely in the absence of proof qualified by the absence of a desire to prove;
therefore, the statement of the second objection is made because the Mīmāṃsaka position does not admit an inference where the probandum (sādhya) is a purely positive (kevalānvayi) property.

We consider this to be correct. Nor [is it the case that] "it possesses existence," and so forth; for the point is that since a difference in pervasion (vyāpti) is necessary due to the distinction between the probandum (sādhya) and the probans (sādhana), the identity of the verbal expression (śabdaikya) is not to be accepted. "An absence of both that is distinct" means an absence of both that is distinct from the individual absences.

And likewise, even though there is a cloth-pot (paṭa-ghaṭa) [in a certain place], the cognition "there is neither cloth nor pot" does not have two absences as its object; rather, it has a distinct absence [of the qualified entity] alone. Thus, the meaning is that the definition is indeed over-exclusive (avyāpti). [This refers to the term] "qualified absence" (viśiṣṭābhāva).

The meaning is: "the absence of fire qualified by the property of being located in the kitchen. Now, one might object: even if one includes an absence whose counter-positive is not delimited by a property that subsists distributively (vaiśiṣṭya-vyāsajyavṛti-dharma), it is possible for a lack of pervasion (avyāpti) to occur in the very same inference—"there is fire because there is smoke"—by taking the absence of this or that particular instance of fire; therefore, why demonstrate a lack of pervasion in a different case?

Dispelling the doubt as to "for what purpose," he says: "here" (*atre*). Now, even if it is stated that "the delimitor of the probans-ness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) is not the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitānavacchedaka*)," the avoidance of the fallacy of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) is still not achieved; for, since the absence of smoke belonging to the kitchen (*mahānasīyavahnayabhāva*) and so forth exists in the mountain (*parvata*), which is the locus of the reason (*hetu*), [the counter-correlativity] of that [absence]...
Because properties such as "being a fire of the kitchen" (*mahānasīyatva*) along with "being smoke-possessing" (*dhūmavattva*) constitute the delimitors (*avacchedaka*).
Nor does being a non-delimitor mean not being a locus for the complete distribution (*paryāpti*) of the delimitorhood;
for the complete distribution of the delimitorhood resides in both [properties] together, but not in each one individually. Thus...

It should not be said that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because since it is impossible for what does not reside in each [individually] to reside in both, it is necessary that each [individual] be the locus of the complete inherence (*paryāpti*) of the delimitingness (*avacchedakatā*) of both. Nor...

It should not be argued that even though there is a delimitorhood (*avacchedakatā*) for each [of the two properties] individually, because this delimitorhood is *vyāsajyavṛtti* (occurring over a composite locus), the absence of the delimitorhood delimited by the relation of *paryāpti* (exhaustive occurrence) is unimpaired in the sense that it possesses the difference from both [properties] individually. For if that were the case, [the definition would fail] in instances such as "there is fire on the mountain Mahānasīya because of smoke."

If it is argued that there would be the contingency of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because the absence of each of the delimitors of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*)— namely, "being in the kitchen" (*mahānasīyatva*) and "being a fire" (*vahnitva*)— as delimited by the absence of a fire in the kitchen exists in each of those two properties respectively, we say: not so.

This is because what is intended [by the definition] is that the delimitor of the pervasion-relation (*vyāpti*) is that which is a delimitor of the pervasion of the locus of the probandumhood (*sādhyatā*), provided that it is not a non-delimiter of the pervasion of the counter-correlativity of the absence that is co-locational with the reason (*hetu*). Thus, although in cases such as "fire-ness is the probandum, smoke is the reason" (*vahnimān dhūmāt*), the probandumhood-delimitation (*sādhyatāvacchedakatā*) of fire-ness (*vahni-tva*) is indeed undelimited (*niravacchinnā*), nevertheless...

The delimitor of the locus of the complete distribution (paryāpti) of the delimitation of the probandumness-restriction is the "individuality" (tadvyaktitva) residing in the property of being a large fire;
and that [individuality] is not the delimitor of the locus of the complete distribution of the delimitation of the counterpositiveness of the absence of a large fire located in the kitchen.
Because a property that subsists in only one [of two things] cannot be the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) for the pervasion (*paryāpti*) of a property that subsists distributively (*vyāsajyavṛti*),

otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the usage "the two spaces" (*ākāśau*). Nor can it be argued that, in cases such as "the jar and the cloth," how could a property subsisting in the jar alone be the delimitor for the pervasion of the duality residing in both the jar and the cloth?

It must be stated that [the property] appears [in the cognition]. For it is accepted that the non-pervasion of duality over the delimitor of the objective (uddeśyatāvacchedaka) occurs only in cases where the delimitor of the objective has a single measure (ekamātra) as its delimiting factor.

In this case, however, the delimiting factor of the objective is simply the duality consisting of both "being from a kitchen" (mahānasīyatva) and "being a mountain" (vahnimatva); thus, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti).

It should be noted as the supreme secret that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of "being non-etiological" (*ananyathāsiddha*) with respect to the probandum of smoke in a kitchen (*mahānasīya-vahni*), which is a case of deviation (*vyabhicārin*). Others,
however, [hold that] regarding the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence (*bhāva*) co-extensive with the reason (*hetu-samānādhikaraṇa*)...

The aforementioned over-narrowness (avyāpti) is to be avoided by incorporating as a qualifier the property of "not being delimited by either the delimitor of the probandum-ness or anything other than it. This is because the counterpositiveness (pratiyogitā) of the absence of a fire belonging to a kitchen (mahānasīya-vahnyabhāva), being delimited by both "fire-ness" and its distinct counterpart "kitchen-ness," does not enter into the definition [as a counterpositive determinant].

Because only the counter-correlativity belonging to the absence of a jar and the like constitutes the definition; the phrase "other than that" (*taditarā*) is used to ensure that the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is included within the definition in the case of a deviant reason (*vyabhicārin*); and the phrase "delimited by the probandum-ness" (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) is used to establish the existence of such counter-correlativity in the case of a valid reason (*saddhetu*). Nor is this [the case] even so...

It is indeed impossible to exclude the absence that is the object of the cognition "there is no possessor of the property of being a mountain qualified by the state of having a fire-possessingness" (*vahnimattvaviśiṣṭavahnimattvavān nāsti*). And if the qualification of "unconditionedness" (*niravacchinnatva*) is introduced as a qualifier for the delimitation of the counter-positive-ness (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatā*), [the following applies].

It should not be argued that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of an instance of deviation (*vyabhicārin*) when "possessing a mountain" (*vahnimattva*) is the delimitor of the probandumness (*sādhyatāvacchedakatā*) because it is the state of possessing a mountain; for since pervasion (*vyāpti*) differs according to the differences in the delimiters of probandumness and so forth,
[the definition] applies only to cases where the delimitor of probandumness is non-delimited (*niravacchinna*).
Because the qualification of "unconditionedness" (niravacchinnatva) must be adopted as a qualifier for the delimitation of counter-positive-ness (pratiyogitāvacchedakatā). And even so,

[the definition would fail] in the case of a valid reason (saddhetu) where the delimitation of the property-to-be-proven (sādhyatāvacchedakatā) is delimited by the property of being "fire-ness" (vahnitvatva).

It should not be argued that there is an over-narrowness (avyāpti) in the definition because it would apply to the absence that is the object of the cognition "there is no possessor of the property of being a mountain qualified by the property of being a mountain qualified by the property of having fire. For, in the definition pertaining to cases where the delimitor of the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka) is delimited by that [property],
the [condition] applies to the delimitation of the counter-positive-ness (pratiyogitāvacchedakatā).
This is because the qualification "not delimited by either that which delimits the deliminator of the probandumness (*sādhyatāvacchedakatāvacchedaka*) or anything other than it" must also be adopted.

Now, even so, in the case of a valid reason (*saddhetu*) where *prameya* (knowable) itself is the deliminator of the probandumness, it is impossible to adopt the aforementioned qualification, because anything other than the *prameya*— which serves as the deliminator of the probandumness— is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*).

If it is argued that in such cases, if that qualification were not included, the definition would incur the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) by taking into account the absence of a jar or other things that possess the property of being knowable (*prameya*), we say no.
For just as in the case where "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*) is the probandum through a mediated relation (*paramparayā*), here too [the qualification applies] through a mediated relation.
They say this because they accept that knowability (*prameyatva*) itself is the delimiting factor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*). Now, one might object:

even if the property of being a genus subordinate to "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) through a mediated relation is the delimiting factor of the probandum, there still exists, by way of a direct relation, the absence of that which is qualified by such a genus-ness in the earth.

To the question, "Since the delimitor of the probandum-ness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) is not the non-delimiter of the counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitā*) of such an absence, how is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) avoided?", he says: "And thus," as in the case of "Earth is possessed of color because of its earth-ness" (*rūpavat pṛthivītvāt*), [the counterpositive] is cognition and so forth which possess color-ness (*rūpatva*) by way of the relation of objectivity (*viṣayitā*).
Since non-existence exists in earth by way of inherence (samavāya), there would arise the fault of over-narrowness (avyāpti); therefore,
it is necessary to include the condition that "the delimitation of the counter-positive-ness is delimited by the relation that delimits the property-to-be-proved-ness" within the definition.

The point is that there is no over-extension (*avyāpti*), because the absence of a delimitation (*avacchedakatā*)— delimited by such a series of relations— is intact in the delimiting factor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*). Now,
it may be objected that it is not appropriate to accept a difference in pervasion (*vyāpti*) based on the difference between the probandum and the probans, according to the method stated above.
Because it is possible for pervasion (*vyāpti*) to be expressed by a single word, he says: "of the knowledge of pervasion.

The intended meaning is as follows: it is established by universal experience that an inference is sometimes of the form "possessing a genus that subsists in fewer instances than color-ness" (*rūpatva*), and sometimes of the form "possessing such a genus."

And since that distinction of causes is not possible without [the cognition of] such a generic property (*jāti*), when such a generic property appears as the delimitor of the predicatedness (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*) [in the inferential cognition], then, in such an inference, the cause is the knowledge regarding the property that delimits the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) as being indirectly non-delimiting.

But when such a generic property (*jāti*) appears as the delimitor of the delimitor of the property to be enjoined (*vidheyatāvacchedakatāvacchedaka*), then, in that such inferential cognition, the cause is the knowledge that [the generic property] is not the non-delimiter of the delimitation of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatānavacchedakatva*) with respect to the property that is the delimitor of the property to be proven (*sādhyatāvacchedakatāvacchedaka*).

The conclusion rests precisely on the difference in the causal status of the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Thus, it should be understood that in the root text, the phrase "by the difference between the probandum and the probans" (*sādhyasādhanabhedena*) actually means "by the difference between the delimitors of the probandum-ness and the delimitors of the probans-ness" (*sādhyatāvacchedakasādhanatāvacchedakabhedenā*). [Regarding the example] "merely possessing a genus" (*jātimān*): this refers to the inference "possessing fire" (*vahnimān*), and so forth.

The point is that there is a rule that whatever is the cognition of the property-possessor as lacking a delimiting factor (anavacchedakatva) must appear precisely as the delimiting factor of the predicate (vidheyatāvacchedaka). He resolves this by accepting the consequence—namely, "earthness" and so on. [Objection: But if this is so...

Since, in that view, there would be the undesirable consequence of denying the inference "that which possesses a genus subordinate to *rūpatva* (color-ness) is impermanent," he says: "possessing a genus. [He then says] "in that individuality (*tadvyaktitva*)," etc.

This means that if the individuality residing in a blue jar and so forth were taken as the probans (*hetu*), then there would be the property of being a delimitant of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) of an absence residing in that very individual.

The sense is that [the definition] is sublated in the case of the universal (jāti) such as blueness and so on. Now, one might object: the statement of non-pervasion (avyāpti) in the root-text regarding the argument "it is a substance because of qualified existence" (viśiṣṭasattvāt) is inconsistent, since inherence (samavāya) serves as the delimiting relation for the probans (hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha), and by that relation...

Because "existent-ness" (*satā*) is not the intended subject (*alakṣya*), as it is inconstant (*vyabhicārin*) due to its presence in a quality (*guṇa*) which lacks the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavat*), since [existent-ness] is not distinct from "qualified existent-ness" (*viśiṣṭasatā*). And if the locus delimited by the nature of qualified existent-ness (*viśiṣṭasatātvāvacchinnādhikaraṇatā*) itself were the relation delimiting the reason (*hetutāvacchedakasambandha*).

And by that [qualification], its state of being the definiendum consists in its being enveloped by qualities (*guṇa*). Nor should it be argued: "In this way, let mere existence (*sattāmātra*) be the cause through that relation; for if existence qualified by that relation were the cause, there would be the fault of a redundant qualification (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatā*). This is because [the qualification serves to exclude] the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) of pure existence.

It is stated that [the definition] is not accepted because [the locus] does not possess a qualified existence. Then, one might object that since the non-pervasion (avyāpti) is avoided simply by introducing the relation that delimits the probanshood (hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha), the introduction of the property that delimits the probanshood (hetutāvacchedaka-dharma) is redundant. Anticipating this, [it is replied that] inherence (samavāya) alone is the relation that delimits the probanshood.

Therefore, by that relation, the occurrence in that which possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavadvṛttitva*) is not the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) that serves as the cause for non-being-a-lakṣya; rather,

it is precisely the possession of the delimiting property of the causehood (*hetutāvacchedaka*), which delimits the non-inherence (*anādheyatā*) delimited by that relation as qualified by the locus of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavan-nirūpita*).

He resolves [the objection] by stating "And not... and so forth, [arguing that] there is no deviation (vyabhicāritva) regarding qualified existence (viśiṣṭasattva). "And not... qualified by the delimitor of the probans-hood" means that the very locus of that [non-existence] is existence itself as qualified by the nature of qualified existence (viśiṣṭasattātva), which serves as the delimitor of the probans-hood.

The sense is that [the definition] applies to a quality as well. Since the previously mentioned types of non-pervasion (avyāpti) do not exist in the case of the non-pervasion just demonstrated, the interpretation of "tathaiva" (in the same way) as meaning "similarity" is untenable; therefore, he says: "it remains in that very state.
And thus: in reality, there is the property of being non-co-locus with the counter-positive (pratiyogivyadhikaraṇatva).

The qualification applies specifically to the reason (*hetu*). That [qualification] consists in its subsisting in a locus that is not the locus of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*); the subsistence in the locus of the reason as qualified by that is the qualification of the absence (*abhāva*). Thus, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the qualification of the absence is simply its subsistence in the locus of the reason which is not the locus of the counter-positive.

We consider it reasonable that the intention of the author of the root-text is that it is appropriate to state [the definition] as "heaviness" (*gaurava*). As for the phrase "as heaviness": now, in a case where fire is the probandum (*sādhya*) by means of a conjunction whose counter-positive is water, there [the absence of] a jar and so forth is not [the probans].

[The definition fails] because, by the relation that delimits the probandumness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*), there is no established locus for that which is delimited by the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*tat-pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Nor should it be argued that only the absence of each individual instance of fire (*tattad-vahni-vyakti-abhāva*) constitutes the factor within the definition.

In cases such as "this [subject] possesses color (rūpavān), because it is earth (pṛthivītva)," since it is necessary to include the condition of being delimited by the relation constituting the *sādhyatāvacchedakatā* (the delimiting factor of the probandum-ness) within the *pratiyogitāvacchedakatā* (the delimiting factor of counter-positive-ness)— in order to avoid the fallacy of under-extension (*avyāpti*) that arises from taking the absence of that which possesses color-ness (*rūpatva*) in terms of the relation of objectivity (*viṣayitā*)— [the definition must be modified accordingly].

Because the deliminatorship (avacchedakatā) of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of the absence of that particular individual lacks being delimited by that relation, it does not constitute a part of the definition. Nor is the absence of that which is delimited by a specific generality (vaijātya) inherent in grass and so forth, which serves as the deliminator of the state of being produced [by fire], the one intended in that manner.
It must be stated that [the locus] is established. Even so,

because in the case of a valid reason (saddhetu) where *tadrūpa* is the probandum (*sādhya*) by virtue of its being qualified by inherence (*samavāya*) having that form as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogika*), the locus of the probandum itself is established by that very relation.
If it is argued that this is not so, we reply: no, because relationhood is not admitted in its specific form. However, if that were admitted, then [the definition would be]:

in the generality of relations that delimit the property to be proved (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*), there is the absence of both—(1) having as its counter-positive something delimited by the delimiter of the counter-positiveness of the absence [of the reason], and (2) having as its locus any particular individual that serves as the substratum of the reason (*hetu*).

It must be defined that such an absence itself is "non-occurrent in the same locus as its counter-positive" (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*) within the locus of the reason (*hetvadhikaraṇa*). And in this way, only the absence of a jar and the like is established as being "such.
[This is because] in the conjunction with any particular jar and so forth...

Because the absence of both—the property of having a counter-positive delimited by fire-ness and the property of having a locus such as a mountain—as well as the absence of water, exists in the locus of the reason (the mountain), it would follow that even the absence of water is non-co-locus with its counter-positive in the locus of the reason.
Consequently, there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "Fire is because of smoke"; therefore, the word "general" (*sāmānya*) is included.

The phrase "any whatsoever" (*yatkiṃcit*) is included in order to ensure that the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is a constituent of the definition in the case of a deviant locus (*vyabhicārin*). Therefore, it should be noted that by taking a red-hot iron ball as the "any whatsoever" instance, the absence of both [the probans and the probandum] is established, thereby ensuring that the absence of the probandum is indeed a constituent of the definition. This is so when one accepts that the relation has a specific form (*viśeṣarūpa*).

Where the delimitorship of the property to be proved (*sādhyatāvacchedakatā*) for "largeness" (*vaḍhddhic14;natva*) is by way of inherence (*samavāya*) as the counter-correlative of largeness, there [the definition fails] because the delimitorship of the counter-correlate of the absence co-located with the reason (*hetusamānādhikaraṇābhāvīyapratiyogitāvacchedakatā*), when delimited by the relation constituting the delimitorship of the property to be proved, is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*).

Therefore, to avoid under-extension (*avyāpti*), the condition of being delimited by the relation constituting the deliminatorship of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedakatā*) need not be introduced into the deliminatorship of counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatā*); rather,

for the sake of avoiding the aforementioned under-extension, [the condition] should be introduced by means of the essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) belonging to the deliminatorship that is itself delimited by the relation constituting the deliminatorship of the probandum.

It should be understood that the absence of the property of being a delimitant of counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) is what is intended to be expressed. This is stated in the root text as "distinct" (*bhinna*). Otherwise, [the following contradictions would arise]: in a place devoid of a jar where fire exists, one would have to say "fire does not exist"; and in a place containing a jar where fire is absent, one would have to say "the jar does not exist."

The sense is that there is no occurrence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogi*). "The intention to express the third [case]" means according to the intention of expressing the non-locus of that which is delimited by whatever delimiting property of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*).
"By the word 'non-counter-positive' (*apratiyogin')"—this is stated with reference to the literal meaning of the root text.

In reality, it should be understood that what is intended by "the non-delimitation of such a counter-correlativity" is precisely this [non-delimitation] with respect to the delimitant of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*). Otherwise, as was previously shown, there would be an under-extension (*avyāpti*) in the very case of "fire because of smoke. Regarding the phrase "and here":

The meaning is this: pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that which is delimited by a property other than the one possessing the reason—a property other than that which is delimited by the property serving as the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*)—in relation to the locus of the reason, by means of the relation serving as the delimitor of the probandum. Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that there is complexity (gaurava) in introducing the distinction of infinite properties that are non-limiting adjuncts (*anavacchedaka*) of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*); for, according to the view that a heavy property (*gurudharma*) is not a limiting adjunct of counter-correlativity, the difference from a "conch-necked" entity (*kambugrīvādimadbheda*)— which is itself composed of such a heavy property— is likewise unestablished (*aprasiddhi*), resulting in parity (*sāmya*).

"Bhāvaḥ | Abhāvīyaviśeṣaṇatā" means spatial locative determination (daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā); its meaning is not "locative determination having non-existence as its counter-positive. For if that were the case, then temporal locative determination would also have non-existence as its counter-positive.
Because its exclusion is impossible; this should be understood similarly in what follows. The meaning is that there is an absence of difference from Mahākāla.

Now, one might object: although there is no difference from Mahākāla in Mahākāla by way of spatial qualification (*daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā*), there is no obstacle to the existence of a pot qualified by difference from Mahākāla in that [Mahākāla] by way of temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*).

In response to the doubt that [the relation] might be the one by virtue of which it serves as the locus of the universe, he says: "by way of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and "as a qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*). This means: by way of the two relations—the relation having the qualifier and the qualified as its relata (*pratiyogin*), and the relation itself.
[The phrase] "subsisting in Great Time alone" (*mahākālātmavṛtti*) means: being the probandum (*sādhya*) by way of being a qualifier whose relatum (*anuyogin*) is Great Time.

This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "due to non-establishment" (*aprasiddheḥ*): although even in that case, when the absence of the counter-positive—which is composed of the previously mentioned absence of both—is introduced, the absence of ether (*gaganābhāva*) alone is established, nevertheless, [this is not so] because ether and the like [are related] by way of the temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*).

The state of being a prior-occurrent (pūrvavṛttitva) certainly exists [in the case of the Great Time]; otherwise, the causality of sound and so forth—which is constituted by prior-occurrence—would not exist in space and the like.
As for the claim that [the Great Time] does not reside [in those things], it is simply because it does not reside through any relation other than temporal or spatial qualification (viśeṣaṇatā).

The sense is that for this very reason, the root text—"is considered the substratum of the worlds"—is also consistent. Now, an objection: is the definition formulated as the absence of both [properties] having the state of being a counter-positive as its locus purposeless, given that the counter-positive's non-co-existence is introduced by means of the relation that delimits the counter-positiveness?

Anticipating the objection that the non-existence of a jar and so forth can be established through *samavāya* (inherence) and other relations, [the author] states that even if it were so stated, in order to avoid the fault of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) by taking the absence of fire in the form of *samavāya*, the definition of "counter-positiveness" (*pratiyogitā*) in the subsequent passage...

He provides the resolution with the words "atra" (here), [arguing that] since it is necessary to include the property of being delimited by the relation that delimits the probandumhood (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*), there remains the same defect of under-extension (*avyāpti*) because such a counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitva*) belonging to the absence of a jar and so forth, as delimited by inherence (*samavāya*), is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*).

By demonstrating the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) when only one of the two absences is introduced, he renders the introduction of both absences meaningful—this is indicated by the words "by inherence" (*samavāyena*). He renders the word "universal" (*sāmānya*) meaningful as a means of excluding over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*)—this is indicated by the words "by conjunction" (*saṃyogena*). [The phrase] "having placed in the heart" (*hṛdi nidhāya*) means that since this specific meaning has not yet been stated, it is for the purpose of indicating this very meaning.

The intended meaning is that this has been stated in brief. Now, one might object: the cognition "that which possesses a shell-like neck and so forth does not exist" indeed apprehends delimitation (*avacchedakatva*); however, that [delimitation] is not of the nature of an essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*), but rather consists in non-occurrentness elsewhere (*anatiriktavṛttitva*). Furthermore, even that does not consist in non-occurrentness in that which is devoid of the counter-positive-delimiter (*pratiyogitāvacchedakaśūnya*).

If that were the case, it would follow that there is the cognition "there is no existence in a quality," because the absence of qualified existence (viśiṣṭasattā) exists in a quality, and because existence (sattātva) does not reside in that which is devoid of qualified existence. Rather, however—

The state of being such [an absence] consists precisely in having as its delimiting property of counterpositiveness (pratiyogitāvacchedaka) that which delimits the pervasion (vyāpakatāvacchedaka) of what is delimited by itself. Precisely because the state of being the delimitor of the pervasion of what is delimited by "existent-ness" (sattā) is absent in "qualified existent-ness" (viśiṣṭasattātva), there is no undesirable consequence (āpatti) of the cognition "there is no existence in a quality. Nor [is there such a consequence] in the case of a locus possessing a jar.
There would follow the undesirable consequence that the cognition "that which possesses a conch-like neck and so forth does not exist" would be impossible;
for the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of the absence residing in a pot is not the delimitor of the pervasion delimited by the state of possessing a conch-like neck and so forth.
Nor is there [such] a delimitor of the pervasion delimited by the state of possessing a conch-like neck and so forth.

Alternatively, one might claim that what must be expressed is the state of not being a delimiting factor for the counterpositiveness of an absence that is co-located with that [delimiting property]; however, even so, the problem of non-establishment remains as it was,

because [the property of] being the delimiting factor for the counterpositiveness of an absence co-located with a jar is simpler than [the property of] being the delimiting factor for the counterpositiveness of an absence co-located with that [delimiting property].

It should not be argued that because the property of being the delimitation of the counterpositiveness of an absence residing in that which possesses a conch-like neck (i.e., a tortoise) is too cumbersome (*guru*), an absence delimited by it is unestablished, and therefore the aforementioned delimitation [of counterpositiveness] involving that [property] is impossible.

If it is argued that this is not so, because the collection of differences from whatever serves as the delimitor of the counter-positiveness of an absence that is co-referential with [the property] such as "having a conch-like neck" must be accepted as the delimitor of pervasion, and because that [collection] is well-known—[we reply: do not say so; for by the cognition "there is no jar,"...

It must be stated that the status of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) for potness and the like is established as consisting in a relation of essential identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*). And in that case, since the pot is construed with the absence— which is the meaning of the negative particle— by way of the relation of being the qualificandhood delimited by potness, such a cognition [arises].

Just as the cognition "there is no pot" serves as the means of knowledge (*māna*) for the delimiting nature (*avacchedakatva*) of potness, because it involves the apprehension of potness as a delimitant, so too, how could the cognition "there is no [thing] possessing a conch-shaped neck and so forth" serve as the means of knowledge for the delimiting nature of "possessing a conch-shaped neck and so forth," since that cognition does not involve the apprehension of such a delimiting nature?

Since such a state of being a delimiting factor (avacchedakatva) is the object of that cognition, this [cognition] also apprehends a state of being a delimiting factor— which is indeed of the nature of an essential relation (svarūpa-sambandha)—
in the possession of the neck and so forth, as in the case of "the jar does not exist"; therefore, by the force of that [cognition], even the non-heavy [substance] [is established].

This is because the author’s intention is that [the property] is the delimitant (*avacchedaka*) of the counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitā*). Nor is there any contradiction regarding the nature of delimitation as an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) in a heavy property (*gurudharma*); for, in the aforementioned cognition, [the relation] is indeed through the relation of counterpositiveness delimited by that which delimits the pervasiveness of itself.

It should not be argued that while a positive relation (*anvaya*) is accepted when there is no counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), in cases such as "the jar does not exist," it is more appropriate to accept the relation of the jar and so forth through the relation of counter-correlativity delimited by jar-ness (*ghaṭatvāvacchinnapratiyogitā-sambandha*), on account of parsimony (*lāghava*).

In two cognitions having the same form, in one case there is the apprehension of a relation of counterpositiveness delimited by a property serving as the qualifier in the aspect of the counterpositive,
