while in the other case there is the apprehension of a relation of counterpositiveness delimited by a property that delimits the pervasion of such a [qualifying] property.

Since it is more appropriate to assume, on the grounds of parsimony, that in both cases there is an apprehension of the relation of counterpositiveness as delimited by the property serving as the qualifier of the counterpositive— rather than assuming such a complex construction— it is difficult to find any evidence for the claim that a cumbersome property cannot function as a delimitor.
It should be noted that the delimiting nature (*avacchedakatā*) must be accepted as being established solely in accordance with conventional usage (*pratīti*).

Now, one might object: in a definition composed of a double absence (*ubhayābhāva*) whose locus is the counter-positive (*pratiyogitā*), there can be no suspicion at all of the defect of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) regarding a probandum (*sādhya*) delimited by a cumbersome property (*gurudharma*), because [such a cumbersome property]...
If it is asked, "How can this be so, given that the status of being a delimitor (*avacchedakatā*) of the probandumness (*sādhyatā*) is impossible?"— the answer is: no,

because the ancients do not accept a delimitorship in the form of an essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*) for a heavy property (*gurudharma*), [and thus such a status of being a delimitor of the probandumness does not exist].

The core point is that since even a cumbersome property (*gurudharma*) can possess that [status] by virtue of being a specific form of objectivity (*viṣayatā*), [the definition holds]. Regarding the phrase "pakṣavṛttitvam" (subsistence in the subject) in the root text, the word "iti" must be supplied as the answer to the question "kimiti" (why?).
Thus, *pakṣatva* (subjecthood), which constitutes the subsistence in the subject, is the object of one's desire to know (*majjijñāsā*).

The meaning is that for this reason, he states its status as the subject (*pakṣatva*). Now, in response to the doubt—"What connection has been demonstrated by this much?"—he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). [Objection: Granted that there is a connection by way of introduction (*upoddhāta*) in defining the subject-status (*pakṣatā*) immediately after the definition of the reflective cognition (*parāmarśa*).

To address the question of what the connection is for the determination of *pakṣatā* immediately following the determination of pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says: "The determination of pervasion... and so forth. "Performing a single effect" means being the motivator (*prayojaka*) of a single effect. And as for being a motivator...

This is common to both the cause and that which delimits the causal status. Therefore, even though *pakṣatā* (the state of being the subject) is a cause for inference, and even though *vyāpti* (pervasion) serves as the delimiter of the causal status by way of being its object, there is no deficiency.
For this very reason, [the definition follows] immediately after the description of the valid logical reason (*saddhetu*).

Even in the investigation of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), the demonstration of the connection through the performance of a single function by the authors of the *Dīdhiti* is consistent; for, from the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of one's own stated valid reason, an inference is produced,
while [the same result is prevented] by the cognition of the defectiveness of another's stated counter-reason (*pratihetu*).

Furthermore, it is because [the topic] is useful for inference by way of removing obstacles. In reality, even the introductory section (upoddhāta) indeed constitutes a lack of topical connection (*asaṅgati*) with the determination of pervasion (*vyāpti*),
since it is the state of being the object of a cognition that generates a desire to know the reason why it should be mentioned immediately after that [determination of pervasion].
Because that [pakṣadharmatā] is defined by its connection with that [vyāpti],

even after the determination of pervasion (vyāpti), there arises the possibility of generating a desire for knowledge— namely, "What is pakṣatva, which is a constituent of 'subsistence in the subject' (pakṣavṛttitva)"— upon the recollection of subsistence in the subject as being the object of a single act of reflective awareness (parāmarśa). For this very reason...

After the determination of the nature of *pakṣatā* (the state of being the subject of inference), Gadādharabhaṭṭācārya has established that the introduction to the definition of inference stated by Raghunātha Śiromaṇi (Dīdhiti) possesses a logical connection (*saṅgati*) as determined by the determination of *pakṣatā*, specifically in the context of establishing the causality of *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection).

The object of meditation (*dhyeya*). Regarding the phrase "with clarity": even if one were to state that "the subject (*pakṣa*) is that wherein there is an absence of proof qualified by the absence of a desire to prove," it would still be possible to arrive at the meaning that "such an absence is the subject-hood (*pakṣatā*). Therefore, the term "with clarity" was employed. Regarding the phrase "lest there be the consequence of under-extension (*avyāpti*"): [in the case of] the subject...

The meaning is "due to the occurrence of the absence of *pakṣatā* (the state of being a subject). Nor should it be argued that even though the *siddhi* (established knowledge) qualified by the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) exists in the person by way of inherence (*samavāya*), there would still be the consequence of *pakṣatā* because its absence exists in the *pakṣa* (subject), since the intended meaning is that [the qualification] "subsists" by way of the relation of qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā*). Therefore...

The meaning is that [the suffix] *asi* ends in the fourth case (*caturthyanta*). "At one time" (*ekakāle*) means at one moment (*ekakṣaṇa*); by this, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) based on taking a gross duration of time. "When the opposite exists" (*virodhisattve*) means when the obstructer exists.

"There would be a desire to infer" (*anumitsā syāt*) means that the desire to infer would persist. Otherwise, in the absence of the *parāmarśa* (the intermediate inferential cognition), inference itself would not arise.

Since there is no basis for postulating that the desire to prove (*sisādhayisā*) acts as an excitant (*uttejaka*), the excitant must be postulated only for the purpose of producing the effect when an obstacle (*pratibandhaka*) is present;
whereas in the absence of proof, [the effect occurs] simply due to the absence of the obstacle.

The point is that since only an excitant (anukūla) is required for the possibility of producing the effect [of inference], one must consider what could be conceived as the excitant when the subject (dharmin) is non-existent due to the absence of the desire to prove (siṣādhayiṣā),
both at the time of the attainment of the conclusion and at the time of mere consideration (parāmarśa). Regarding the desire to prove:

Because [the inference] would arise from the possibility [of the reason being present], the root text stating "at the time of the establishment [of the probandum]" and so forth is incoherent; therefore, he explains it with the word "siddhi" (establishment).
Now, one might object: immediately after the perception that "the mountain possesses smoke pervaded by fire," the very desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) cannot possibly occur.

Because there is an absence of the cognition that [the action] is a means to achieve what is desired, and since the cognition that it is a means to achieve what is desired is the cause of the desire for the means, if one were to admit such a cognition prior to the perception [of the object],
then the perception itself would not be possible due to the obstruction caused by the causal complex of a powerful desire.

To dispel the doubt that, upon the acceptance [of inference] immediately after perception, the perception itself would no longer persist at the moment of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), he completes the sentence with "inference," and so forth.
The term "indicative" (*paricāyaka*) refers to the entire sequence ending with "there is inference" provided that there is both desire and the absence of established knowledge (*siddhi*).
The meaning is that it brings about the knowledge of specific instances of desire as qualified by their respective individualities (*tattadvyaktitva*).

By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "only as their respective individualities," the inclusion of the portion ending with "inference" (*anumiti*) within the scope of the determinant of the inciter (*ujjīvakatāvacchedaka*) is excluded. Now, one might object: a desire such as "let some knowledge arise" is not possible when [the object] is already established.

Because desire does not arise toward an object that is already established, since some degree of knowledge of it has been attained; nor should it be argued that there is no logical inconsistency because desire is observed even during a state of ignorance regarding something already established—
since desire does not arise even for a manifested individual instance of knowledge and so forth when there is an absence of the cognition of its being already established.

According to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the cognition of [an object] as already accomplished (*siddhatvajñāna*) is an obstacle only in cases other than knowledge (*jñāna*) and the like; however, in the case of knowledge and so forth, mere accomplishment (*siddhi*) is the contradictory factor. For this very reason, the authors of various treatises have stated in various places, "Because there is an absence of desire for what is already accomplished. Therefore, he explains: "That which occurs subsequent to this," and so on.

Regarding the phrase "when the causal complex for inference (*anumiti-sāmagrī*) is present": in the absence of the causal complex for inference, it is impossible to accept the desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) of an inference occurring by the force of such a desire; whereas when that [complex] is present, because there is the presence of the subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) and so forth, as well as the causal complex for mental perception (*mānasa-sāmagrī*) belonging to the self...

The point is this: even with the arising of such a mental [desire], inference cannot arise because the object of the desire has already been established; therefore, it is accepted that only that specific kind of desire for which the object is not established without inference serves as the "excitant" (ujjūka). Now, an objection: [nanu...]

Immediately after the perception "the mountain possesses smoke that pervades fire," by the force of the desire "let there arise a cognition of fire distinct from the perception [of the smoke]," an inference (*anumiti*) of fire becomes possible.
To dispel the doubt that even through a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) regarding fire, there is the possibility of fulfilling the object of such a desire,
he completes the sentence with "in the absence of the causal complex for verbal cognition" (*śābda-sāmagrī-asattve*), and so forth. Thus,
since at that time a verbal [cognition] of fire is impossible, [the desire is fulfilled] by inference alone.

The intended meaning is that the accomplishment of the object occurs. "From the manifestation of the desire for that" means from the manifestation of the desire, "May I infer fire by means of light," which exists at the time of the consideration (*parāmarśa*) of smoke.

"Because it does not act as an intensifier" means that it does not act as an intensifier of the counter-positiveness of the absence which serves as the delimiting factor for the counter-restriction of the obstructiveness of an inference whose objective is delimited by "mountain-ness," whose predicate is delimited by "fire-ness," and whose logical mark is delimited by "smoke-ness. This is because [the smoke] is not the counter-positive of such an absence that possesses the aforementioned delimiting factor.

Up to: "by way of being a desire for the object of an inference. If it were stated as "having an inferentiality (anumititva)-delimited qualificandum," then [the following would arise]: "May there be for me a cognition having a mountain as its subject and fire as its qualificandum."

The desire "may it arise" and so forth would not be included [in the definition], and thus they are excluded. Furthermore, even if such a desire acts as an excitant (*uttejaka*), when there is already a proof (*siddhi*),
at the time when there is a causal complex for perception and the like that has a mountain as its object and fire as its qualificandum—
It should not be argued that such a desire leads to the undesirable consequence of such an inference [arising in perception],

because in the case of perception, the status of being the subject (*uddeśyatva*) and the predicate (*vidheyatva*) are not established by valid means of knowledge (*aprāmāṇika*). Nor is it the case that the inclusion of "being within the scope of an inference" is redundant for such a desire.
It should not be said that [the definition] is too narrow because it applies only to the object of inference (*anumiti*);

for that [qualification] is necessary to prevent the undesired consequence of an inference arising from the force of a discordant desire such as, "May there arise a perception whose qualificandum is the mountain and whose predicate is fire."

Nor should it be argued that, even so, since both the status of being the subject (*uddeśyakatva*) and the status of being the predicate (*vidheyakatva*) are admitted in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), there would be the unwanted consequence of an inference (*anumiti*) occurring when the causal complex for such a verbal cognition exists— even if a proof (*siddhi*) is present— due to the force of such a desire. For in the verbal cognition "the mountain possesses fire," fire itself is the qualifier (*prakāra*) in relation to the mountain by way of identity (*tādātmya*).

This is because the vidheyatā (the property of being the predicate) delimited by *vahni-tva* (fire-ness), as determined by an uddeśyatā (the property of being the subject) delimited by *parvata-tva* (mountain-ness), is not present there.

For it must be accepted that the instigator [of the desire] is a desire whose object is an inference characterized by a *prakāratā* (the property of being a qualifier) consisting in having such a *vahni-vidheyatā*. Now, even so, [one might argue] that fire is known on the mountain through identity (*tādātmyena*).
At the time when there is a verbal causal complex (*śābdasāmagrī*) having as its object of prescription (*vidheya*) fire on a mountain,
even if there is already proof (*siddhi*),
there arises a cognition characterized by a subjecthood (*uddeśyatā*) delimited by "mountain-ness" (*parvatatva*) and a predicatehood (*vidheyatā*) delimited by "fire-ness" (*vahnimatva*).
If it is argued that [the cognition] "let there be smoke" would arise from this desire because it has a mountain as its objective (uddeśya) and fire as its qualificand (vidheya),

we say no; for even in verbal comprehension (śābdabodha), if one accepts objective-ness (uddeśyatā) and qualificand-ness (vidheyatā), then such desires would likewise result in an inference where fire is the qualificand.

Since the status of being an excitant (ujjñaka) must be accepted as belonging to that very individuality, it is improper to accept complexity (gaurava) in a case where a simpler means (laghūpāya) is possible. In fact, regarding verbal cognition...

Being an object of prescription (*vidheyatva*) and so forth are indeed unauthenticated. Their acceptance is necessary only in the case of inference (*anumiti*); otherwise, there would arise the undesirable consequence of such expressions as "I infer the mountain" being used with the intention of expressing the inference "the mountain possesses fire."

This is because, even if elsewhere the second case suffix (*dvitīyā*) has "objectness" (*viṣayitva*) as its meaning, when used in conjunction with a verbal root whose meaning is "inference," it is possible to avoid such an application by accepting that "prescribability" (*vidheyatva*) is the meaning of the second case and "subjecthood" (*uddeśyatva*) is the meaning of the locative case (*saptamī*), provided that the inference possesses prescribability and so forth. Nor should it be argued that "being the qualifier" (*prakāritva*) alone should be the meaning of the second case there.
It should not be argued that even by that much, the possibility of using expressions such as "I infer the mountain" is excluded;

for even so, there would still result the undesirable consequence of such cognitions as "I infer mountain-ness. For this very reason, Gadādharabhaṭṭācārya stated that when used in conjunction with a verbal root having the sense of inference (*anumiti*), [the suffixes denote] the state of being the object to be enjoined (*vidheyatva*) and the state of being the agent of enjoining (*vidheyitva*).

Or, it is the meaning of the accusative case. However, when used in conjunction with a verbal root whose meaning is verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), there is no harm even if objecthood (*viṣayitva*) is the meaning of the accusative; for the usage "I hear the mountain" (*parvataṃ śṛṇomi*) is accepted as valid.
But in the case of the locative case, it is always [the meaning] when used in conjunction with a verbal root other than one whose meaning is inference (*anumiti*).

The meaning [of the locative case] is precisely the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*). If it is considered that, this being the case, there would arise the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of using the expression "I hear the mountain on the mountain," because even a verbal cognition having the mountain as its qualificand possesses the mountain as its object,
then [the rule applies] in cases where there is co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with a word ending in the seventh case.

Let it be understood that the meaning of the accusative case is simply the state of being a qualificand (prakāritā) as delimited by a relation other than identity (*tādātmya*). Because of the inclusion of the term "other" (*atirikta*), expressions such as "I hear fire on the mountain" (*parvate vahnimantaṃ śṛṇomi*) do not occur.
Now, even so, in the state of merely having a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of smoke—

By the force of the desire, "Let there arise an inference based on smoke as the logical mark (*liṅga*) which has as its object the mountain and as its predicate (*vidheya*) fire," there would follow the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of an inference based on smoke as the logical mark having fire as its predicate.

This is because such a desire also possesses the property of having the aforementioned predicate (fire) as its qualifier (*prakāra*) and because it has the inferential cognition itself as its object (*viṣaya*). Nor is this [the case]...

It should not be argued that the qualification "not having a particular linga as its cause" (kiṃcilliṅgakatvāprakārakatva) must also be included as a qualifier of the desire, so that there is no occurrence of the aforementioned inference by the force of such a desire; for if that were the case, [the definition would fail] even when there exists a desire such as: "Let there arise an inference having smoke as its linga and possessing a particular fire as its vidheya."

Otherwise, there would be no inference based on the mark "smoke" (*dhūmaliṅgaka*). Nor can it be said that, for an inference whose mark is delimited by a particular property (*taddharmāvacchinnaliṅgakānumiti*), the desire or the effort that prompts it must necessarily have as its object a mark not delimited by any other property (*tadanyadharmāvacchinnaliṅgakatvāprakārika*).

It must be stated that [the definition] succeeds in including a desire whose qualifier is the state of having smoke as its logical mark (*dhūmaliṅgakatva*), while excluding a desire whose qualifier is the state of having a different logical mark (*bhinnaliṅgakatva*). Even so, [there remains the problem of] such [a desire] where the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is fire...

It might be argued that both an inference based on the mark of smoke (*dhūmaliṅgakānumiti*) and an inference based on the mark of light (*ālokaliṅgakānumiti*) should arise simultaneously because of the presence of a desire for both; however, this is not so, because it is impossible to bring about an inference based on the mark of smoke [simultaneously with one based on light]. This is because the causal efficacy of a desire must be accepted as residing in its being a desire characterized by a subject-locus (*viśeṣyatā*) belonging to an inference, which is qualified by a mode (*prakāratā*) having as its qualifier the property of having a probandum (*vidheya*) limited by a specific property (such as fire), and which is not qualified by a mode having as its qualifier the state of being an inference whose mark is limited by a property other than that specific property.

However, in the case of an inference based on a desire for a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*), there are two distinct objective determinants (*viśeṣyatā*): one is determined by a mode (*prakāratā*) consisting of having smoke as the inferential mark (*dhūmaliṅgakatva*), and the other is determined by a mode consisting of having light as the inferential mark (*ālokaliṅgakatva*). In a collective apprehension, the objective determinants differ precisely because their modes are distinct; otherwise, [the cognition] would be "a tree" [rather than a specific judgment].

There would be no distinction between the aggregate cognition "the tree possesses monkey-contact and lacks it" and the doubt "is the tree in contact with a monkey or not," because even in a collective representation (samūhālambana) whose qualificandum is delimited by a single property, there is a difference based on the distinctness of the objective modes (prakāratā).
The distinction between the qualificanda (viśeṣyatā) would not be a [real] difference;

for even in a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*) where the qualificandum is delimited by a single property, there is a distinction between the qualificanda based on the distinction between the modes (*prakāratā*),
whereas in a doubt, there is a single qualificandum determined by two modes.

Because of the difference between those two. And thus, the property of being an inference based solely on the mark of smoke (*dhūmamātra-liṅgaka-anumiti*) must be stated as the delimitor of the effectness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) of the absence of proof (*siddhi*) qualified by the absence of such a desire. Otherwise, [from] both the parāmarśas of smoke and light...

Otherwise, by the force of a desire that apprehends the qualification of one thing by another— such as "let there arise an inference having light as its probans (liṅga)"— there would result the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the absence of the aforementioned proof (siddhi) in such an inference, because it would occur even when there is no inference having smoke as its probans. Alternatively,
the qualification of the desire should be taken as simply "not having 'having some probans' as its qualifier."

Since it must be postulated that a desire whose mode is "having smoke as its probans" (dhūmaliṅgakatva) possesses a distinct excitatory power (uttejakatva), the failure to include such cases is not a defect; enough of this prolixity. Such a state of established knowledge (siddhi) existing, there is no inference [of the form] "the mountain possesses fire."

If it is stated that such a *siddhi* (established cognition) is an inhibitor of such an inference (*anumiti*), then even a *siddhi* in the form "the mountain possesses fire" would not be an inhibitor of such an inference,
because an inference still arises through the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) even when such a *siddhi* exists. Therefore—

It was stated: "the desire to prove" (*siṣādhayiṣā*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "delimited by mountain-ness" (*parvatatvāvacchinna*): the expression "absence of the desire to prove" (*siṣādhayiṣāviraha*) and the like is merely a defining characteristic (*paricāyaka*); otherwise, the term "specifically" (*viśiṣya*) would be rendered redundant—this is the intended meaning.
Even when the causal complex for a perception (*pratyakṣasāmagrī*) concerning a different object is present, [the desire to prove]...

He shows that the phrase "the causal complex of perception" (*pratyakṣasāmagrī*) refers to the causal complex of a perception having the same object, because inference arises even without it—by the words "by that" (*tena*). [Objection:
But surely, at the time when there is visual contact with fire and so forth, [one perceives] "the mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire."

One might ask: why was it not stated in the root text that for one possessing such knowledge, there is perception and not inference? Why was this said instead in accordance with cases where perception occurs subsequent to doubt?

To dispel this doubt, he says: "In such cases" (*etādṛśa*). This means "in the case of that object," i.e., in the case of the object of perception. The sense of the locative case here is "having as its object."
And its positive concomitance (anvaya) is in that inference;

thus, the meaning is that it is for the purpose of demonstrating the causal complex (sāmagrī) for an inference whose object to be proven (sādhya) is an object of perception. "Independently" means not being included within the causal complex of perception.

Regarding the phrase "prayāsāpatteḥ": the sense is that since the demonstration of both causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) is established by the mere demonstration of one causal complex, it is improper to demonstrate the causal complexes separately. Now, [one might ask]: if the causal complex of perception acts as an obstructor because it enters into the scope of the "subjectness" (*pakṣatā*), what [is the consequence]?

On the contrary, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) precisely in its being a sublater because it enters into the scope of the *pakṣatā* (the state of being the subject of inquiry); for [the opponent] might object that parsimony lies simply in the fact that there is only one sublater, since this is sufficient for the explanation. To refute this doubt, [the author states that] a single sublater is not even possible.

He says "śābda" etc., because it must be stated that the capacity to act as an excitant (utejakatva) resides in the causal complex (sāmagrī) for the establishment of the will (icchā) in its various distinct forms. The meaning is: [the will] produced by the verbal cognition arising from sentences such as "the mountain is blue. The mountain...
It should be understood that the established cognition (*siddhi*) produced by sentences such as "the jar is eternal" does not constitute an obstacle [to inference].
Regarding the phrase "by way of being an intention whose object is the aforementioned inference":
this means by way of the specific individuality (*tadvyaktitva*) residing in the intention whose object is the aforementioned inference.

It should be noted that this is because it was previously stated that for those whose desires do not follow [the rule], their status as an excitant (*uttejaka*) is determined solely by their individuality (*tadvyaktitvena*). Regarding the phrase "by the non-arising of inference": the sense is that such a desire can have its object established by perception alone.

Regarding the phrase "by way of being an inclination whose qualifier is the nature of being an inference" (*anumititva-prakāraka-icchātvena*): although this being the case, at the time when the causal complex for the perception of fire is present, an inference of fire would not arise from an inclination such as "let there be a cognition other than perception," nevertheless, [the definition applies] even by way of being an inclination whose qualifier is the state of being other than perception (*pratyakṣānyatva-prakāraka-icchātvena*).
There is no fault, because the status of being an excitant (uttejaka) must be postulated for the causal complex of perception.
Regarding the phrase "consisting of eye-contact and so forth": although mere eye-contact is not the causal complex, nevertheless, by virtue of the relation of occurring in the same moment...

It should be understood that the possibility of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consists in the visual contact being qualified by the cognition of the qualifier belonging to that person (*tatpuruṣīya*). Regarding the term "of a different class" (*vijātīya*):
the meaning is that it is delimited by a specific class-character (*vaijātya*) which excludes the contact between another self and the mind (*parātmamanaḥsaṃyoga*).
"Independently" means not being included within the scope of the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*).

That is to say, merely by virtue of being the causal complex for perception (*pratyakṣa-sāmagrī*). "Beyond inference" means [being] either that which produces a proof distinct from the inferential cognition produced by the absence of the desire to know (*sādhayiṣā*) qualified by the absence of proof (*siddhi*), or that which produces a proof [other than that].
The final meaning is that [the perception] acts as an obstacle.

It should be understood that according to the literal reading, there would be no possibility of inference for one who possesses visual perception. Now, just as the causal complex for perception (pratyakṣa-sāmagrī) is constituted by the absence of the causal complex for an inference regarding a different object, so too is the causal complex for an inference regarding a different object [constituted by the absence of the causal complex for perception].

Because it is constituted by the absence of the causal complex for perception (*pratyakṣa-sāmagrī*), when there is a coexistence of the causal complexes for perception and inference directed toward different objects, the non-arising of inference would be impossible to resolve; for, since the causal complex for perception acts as an inhibitor with respect to inference, there would be an absence of the causal complex for inference directed toward a different object, being constituted by that very absence. Therefore—

He says: "Or rather" (yadvā) || 70 || [This refers to] the section beginning with "characterized by victory," which follows the determination of valid reasons (*saddhetu*) and precedes the determination of fallacious reasons (*asaddhetu*).
The meaning is that the state of being the cause (*kāritva*)—that is, the state of being the motivator (*prayojakatva*)—of that single effect which is the very nature of the proponent's victory.

The meaning is that in a debate, a proponent achieves victory not only by establishing the soundness of his own stated reason, but also by demonstrating the fallacious nature of the counter-reason put forward by the opponent.

The term "victory" (*vijaya*) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication); it should also be understood that the determination of the true nature of the definition of inference (*anumiti-lakṣaṇa-tattva-nirṇaya*) is likewise one of the effects [of this work]. Regarding the phrase "without the knowledge of a common property" (*sādhāraṇa-dharma-jñānaṃ vinā*): the sense is that the knowledge of a property (*taddharma-jñāna*) is the cause for a desire directed toward an object of knowledge characterized by a subordinate property of that [common] property (*taddharmāvāntara-dharma-prakāraka-jñāna-gocarecchā*). Regarding the term "useless" (*niṣprayojaka*): there is no...
The meaning of "devoid of a motivator" (*prayojakaśūnya*) is derived from the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) of the word *prayojaka* as that in which [something] is the motivator;
the sense is that, regarding the division [of fallacies], the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) alone is the motivator.
As for the definition of a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*), it is based on the etymological analysis of *hetvābhāsa* as "the semblances (*ābhāsa*)—that is, the defects (*doṣa*)—of a reason (*hetu*)."

The meaning is: "the definition of the defects of the reason. Although one might argue that since only defective reasons are being classified, it would be more appropriate to state the definition of a defective reason itself, there is no such fault; for once the defects are known, the definition of defectiveness—consisting in the possession of those defects—can be easily understood. Thus, in the root text...

The term *hetvābhāsān* (fallacious reasons) should be understood as referring exclusively to defective reasons (*duṣṭahetu*), based on the etymological derivation that they "appear like valid reasons" (*hetuvad ābhāsante*). [The phrase] "the absence of fire" refers to the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). Thus, the sense is that even a valid reason (*saddhetu*) may appear as a defective one. [This is expressed by the words] "and not... (*na ca*).

Now, if the inclusion of the *paryāpti* (distributive occurrence) of the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatā*) is introduced, there would indeed be an impossibility (*asaṃbhava*) in the case of [the cognition] "a bhadra possessing the absence of fire," because even though it has as its object a bhadra possessing the absence of fire, it lacks the *paryāpti* of the delimiting factor; this is so because [such a cognition] must be included within the category of non-erroneous, non-artificial certainty (*anāhāryaniścaya*) that is not overridden by a cognition of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyajñāna*).

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because the intended definition is: "thatness which consists in the pervasion of the locus of the delimitation of the obstructiveness (pratibandhakatā) by the state of having as its object that [x] which is accompanied by these three.

For [if this were the case], [obstructiveness] would exist through the state of having a qualified object (viśiṣṭaviṣayakatva), such as [the cognition of] "possessing fire" (vahnimattva), and so forth.

Since it is untenable for an error apprehending *guñjā* (false coral) and the like to function as a sublater, the sublateness must be stated as residing in a cognition characterized by a subject-object relation (*nirūpya-nirūpaka-bhāva*) between its objective contents; therefore, the property of being a collection of [properties such as] having a qualified object (*viśiṣṭa-viṣayakatva*) and so forth is of a narrower extension (*nyūna-vṛtti*).

Because [the definition] lacks the property of being a delimiting factor (*paryāpti*). Nor can it be argued that the very objectivity (*viṣayitā*) existing in a knowledge consisting of valid cognition (*pramā*), which has entered into a relation of the determined and the determiner (*nirūpya-nirūpakabhāva*), is itself the qualified objectivity;
for, by virtue of being an objectivity that has entered into a relation of the determined and the determiner, [all] qualified objectivities...
It must be said that the pervasion (paryāpti) of the delimitation of the obstructive capacity remains intact;
for, by the rule that what does not reside in each individual member does not reside in the aggregate, this ensures the avoidance of over-extension (ativyāpti) to a single part.
Since it is necessary to include the limit of the pervasion of the delimiting relation (*avacchedakatā-paryāpti*),

and because the pervasion of the delimiting relation can in no way possibly exist within the objectivity (*viṣayitā*) of such a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*), he says: "or non-occurrentness beyond [the locus]" (*anatiriktavṛttitvam vā*).
The meaning is as follows: the definition of being a delimiting condition (*avacchedakatva*) of obstructiveness is simply the state of not being excluded from that which is devoid of obstructiveness.

Consequently, since the property of having "the absence of fire" as its qualificative content (*prakārakatva*) and so forth is common even to cognitions whose delimiting condition of the subject (*nirūpakatāvacchedaka*) is non-obstructive, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the absence of fire and the like. [This is established] by the method previously stated.

The meaning is that since the qualified [object] is not distinct from the pure [object], even a cognition such as "lake" (which lacks the obstructing factor) possesses the qualified as its object. In this manner, because there is no occurrence of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) anywhere, the term "over-extension" (*ativyāpti*) refers solely to the presence of *lakṣaṇā*; thus, there is rather "impossibility" (*asaṃbhava*).

Thus it is concluded. Regarding the phrase "delimited by whatever form" (*yadrūpāvacchinna*): [an objection is raised]—if this is so, then that [nature of being a defect] would reside only in things such as a pot (*ghaṭa*) which possess the absence of another, but not in defects such as a pot which possess the absence of another; how then can that [absence] be the definition of a defect? To this [it is replied]:...

He says: "of this [term] 'tattvam'. Now, one might object: by the word *yadrūpa*, only "lake-ness qualified by the absence of fire" (*vahnyabhāvavad-hradatva*) should be grasped; and that, through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), is simply "lake-ness as qualified by the absence of fire," because the suffix following a *karmadhāraya* compound denotes the state of being that very thing.

This is because of the statement in the *Dīdhiti*: "Because it expresses the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two delimiters of the objecthood (*padārthatāvacchedaka*). Furthermore, the objective content (*viṣayitā*) delimited by that [co-occurrence] does not exist in the obstructing cognition, namely in the cognition "the lake possesses the absence of fire," since [the co-occurrence] exists in the property of being a lake (*hradatva*) by way of the relation of co-occurrence.

Because the absence of fire is not a qualifier [of the locus], he says: "delimited by the absence of fire. Thus, in that case, it is the pair consisting of the absence of fire and the property of being a lake (hradatva) alone that is to be grasped by the term *yadrūpa* (whatever form), and not the aforementioned qualified entity.

The point is that [if the definition were formulated as stated], the aforementioned defect would arise; furthermore, even in a non-obstructive cognition such as "the lake possesses a counter-positive-ness qualified by a counter-positive whose delimiting property is absent," there would be an impossibility (asaṃbhava) because the objective content delimited by that specific form exists therein. This applies even to the cognition "the lake."

Because the objective content delimited by *hradatva* (lake-ness) exists, and because the objective content delimited by the absence of fire (*vahnimad-abhāva*) is absent, there is a lack of the objective content delimited by both [conditions].
It is precisely for the purpose of indicating this that the author of the text has demonstrated only the absence of the objective content delimited by the absence of fire, and not...
His intention is that the form graspable by the word "absence" (abhāva) is merely the absence of something else. That being the case,
the objective content delimited solely by the absence of fire (*kevala-vahnyabhāvāvacchinna-viṣayatā*) does not constitute an impediment [to the cognition] "this possesses the absence of fire."

It should be understood that this is because the definition applies by taking "mere absence of fire" (*vahnayabhāvamātra*) as the term *yadrūpa*, since this is common to cognitions where the delimiting property (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) is not determined. Now, in this way,

the state of having an objectivity delimited by both "absence of fire" and "lake-ness" (*vahnayabhāvahradatvobhayāvacchinnaviṣayitva*) is nothing other than being the determiner of a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) that is itself determined by a modehood (*prakāratā*) residing in both "absence of fire" and "lake-ness."

And that [cognition] exists in a cognition where two things are apprehended in a single locus— specifically, in a cognition whose qualificandum is delimited by the absence of fire and whose qualifiers are both "absence of fire" and "lake-ness," according to the principle that "two [things] reside in one."

If it is argued that there is an impossibility (asambhava) because such a subjectivity (viṣayatā) does not reside in what is distinct from the state of being an obstructor (pratibandhakatā)— to this, some say:

"That which is the state of being the determiner (nirūpakatva) of a qualificandumness (viśeṣyatā) delimited by a certain form (yadrūpāvacchinna), as determined by a qualifierhood (prakāratā) delimited by a certain form (yadrūpāvacchinna), resides in no more than the state of being an obstructor of inference (anumitipratibandhakatā)."
Since the intended meaning is that a defect is a locus delimited by a specific form (tadrūpāvaccchinna) which is qualified by another property delimited by that same form (tadrūpāvaccchinnaviśiṣṭa),

the property of being the determiner of a subjecthood delimited by "lake-ness" (hradatvāvaccchinnaviśeṣyatānirūpakatva)— as determined by a modehood delimited by "the state of being an absence of fire" (vahnimadbhāvatvāvaccchinnaprakāratānirūpita)— occurs in a domain no wider than the state of being an impediment to inference. Therefore, a lake delimited by "lake-ness" and qualified by "the state of being an absence of fire" constitutes a defect.

Thus they say; but that is incorrect. For if that were the case, there would follow the consequence of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) with respect to a jar qualified by pure substanceness (*dravyatva*), which is the object of the certainty "the jar is a substance"—a certainty that acts as an obstacle to the inference "the jar is not a substance."

This is because it is impossible to take the property-qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) of "substance-ness" as being delimited by that specific form (*yadrūpa*), since that [property-qualifierhood] is undelimited (*niravacchinna*). However, others hold that by the term "that form" (*yadrūpa*),
one must understand things such as "lake-ness" (*hradatva*) which has attained the status of being the delimiting factor of the locus (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) of the absence of fire.

And the state of being delimited by "lake-ness" (hradatva), which has attained the status of the delimiting factor of the subject (dharmitāvacchedakatāpanna), consists in its own objectivity (svaviṣayitā) having the property of being delimited by the delimiting factor of the subjecthood (dharmitāvacchedakatā) as determined by itself, which in turn is determined by itself. [This is illustrated in the cognition: "The lake possesses the absence of fire."

The state of having as its delimitation of the specifierhood (nirūpakatāvacchedakatā) that which specifies the objecthood (viṣayitā) belonging to the cognition "the lake possesses the absence of fire" is precisely the specifierhood of the objecthood belonging to that cognition,
which is itself specified by the locus-specifierhood (dharmitāvacchedakatā) of the absence of fire.
In the view of those who maintain the difference between the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) and the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in a single cognition,
just as there exists a relation of the defined and the definer (*nirūpya-nirūpaka-bhāva*),

so too does it exist between the state of being a delimiting factor of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedakatva*) and the state of being a delimiting factor of the definiendum of the objecthood (*viṣayitānirūpakatāvacchedakatva*).
The relationship between the object to be determined (*nirūpya*) and the determiner (*nirūpaka*) must be accepted;

for it is precisely in a cognition whose qualificandum is delimited by lake-ness (*hradatva*) and which has the absence of fire as its qualifier, that there occurs the state of having as its object that which is delimited by lake-ness, wherein lake-ness has attained the status of being the delimiting property of the locus (*dharmitāvacchedakatā*) of the absence of fire.
They say it is "in accordance with conventional usage.

However, some maintain that because a cognition possessing both properties—such as being a cow and being a lake—is a *samūhālambana* (a cognition with multiple objects), the objective determinants (*viśeṣyatā*) therein are distinct due to the difference in their respective modes of presentation (*prakāratā*). Thus, [the two are not identical].

In that context, the property of not being the determiner of a subject that is not determined by either of the two modes must be qualified by the condition of not being a non-restrictor of the obstructiveness that is not determined by the relevant inference, in order to exclude the objective content belonging to a cognition whose delimiting property of the subject is "absence of fire" (*vahnayabhāva*).
This applies to the objective content delimited by a specific form (*yadrūpāvacchinnaviṣayitā*) within the aforementioned cognition.

Even though there exists a single objective determination (viśeṣyatā) determined by both modes [of being], it is because that [determination] possesses the status of being the delimiting factor of the obstructiveness (pratibandhakatā) relative to the inference produced by another person, as residing in the cognition "the lake possesses the absence of water. By taking this into account...
They say that there is no such possibility [of over-extension], but that too is incorrect.

For even the objectivity (*viṣayatā*) of "the lake possesses absence of fire" would be a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the obstructiveness (*pratibandhakatā*) determined by the cognition "the lake does not possess absence of fire," which would result in the undesirable consequence of impossibility (*asaṃbhava*).

This is because the nature of being an obstructor (*pratibandhakatā*) varies according to the distinction in the nature of being obstructed (*pratibadhyatā*). Now, [if one were to define the object of obstruction] as that which possesses the objective content (*viṣayitā*) delimited by a specific form, then there would be the consequence of impossibility (*asaṃbhava*), since such objective content exists even in a non-obstructive cognition such as "that which possesses a genus has the absence of fire" (where the genus is apprehended as being *hradatva*), which nevertheless possesses the objective content delimited by that form.

The objectivity delimited by a particular form (*yadrūpāvacchinnaviṣayitā*) should be qualified by the property of belonging to a cognition that is devoid of objectivities delimited by each and every such form (*tattadrūpāvacchinnaviṣayitā*) which is the deliminator of the counter-correlativity of an absence co-located with the state of having as its object that which is delimited by that form. And thus...

Since the definition is perfectly adequate by simply stating that "the defect is that which is delimited by that form which possesses the delimitation— consisting in the essential relation of the objective content delimited by that form belonging to such a cognition"—
the pursuit of a delimitation consisting in "non-occurrence in more than that" (*anatiriktavṛttitva*) is redundant.

If it is argued that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding a single part [of the definition], because the property of having as its object the absence of fire—which belongs to a cognition devoid of the objective content delimited by "lake-ness" (*hradatva*)—is not a determinant of the obstructive power (*pratibandhakatā*), we say: no. [For consider the case of] "Conjunction is possessed of conjunction."

Because over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is unavoidable in the case of that which is qualified by the state of being a conjunction whose object is the locus of sublation (*bādhaviṣaya*), for in that instance,

the objective states (*viṣayitā*) delimited by the nature of conjunction (*saṃyogatva*) are pervasive (*vyāpaka*) of the state of having as their object that which is qualified by the nature of conjunction.

Because, as in the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), since conjunction itself is not established [as a distinct entity], it is impossible to apprehend the objectivity delimited by that [conjunction] as being of the nature of objectivity delimited by a particular form (*yadrūpāvacchinnaviṣayitātva*). Nor is there an objectivity delimited by conjunction that does not pervade the state of having for its content that which is qualified by conjunction; for in that case, there exists [the cognition] of that which possesses conjunction.

It should not be argued that "subjectivity" (viṣayitā) exists there [in the erroneous cognition] because it does not pervade the state of having as its object that which is qualified by the nature of conjunction (saṃyogatva), since conjunction serves as the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) therein; for even in that aforementioned error where conjunction is the qualifier (prakāra) under the aspect of "conjunction-ness" (saṃyogatva), such subjectivity is likewise absent. Now, even if this were so, [regarding] non-existence under the aspect of "non-existence-ness" (abhāvatva)...

Even in the cognition "the lake possesses the absence of fire" (*hradatvāvagāhinyām abhāvavān vahnayabhāvavān*), since there exists a subjectivity delimited by both "fire-absence" and "lake-ness," the condition of being devoid of a subjectivity delimited by any form that serves as the deliminator of the counter-correlativity of an absence co-extensive with the aforementioned subjectivity delimited by both remains unimpaired. This is because, in that case, whatever form delimits the subjectivity that is the deliminator of the counter-correlativity of an absence co-extensive with the subjectivity delimited by both,
the cognition is indeed devoid of a subjectivity delimited by that respective form.

Do not say that this is incorrect, for since the property of being the objecthood delimited by non-existence (*abhāvatvāvacchinnaviṣayitātva*) does not possess that [obstructive] nature, and because such a cognition does not act as an obstacle to inference, the impossibility [of the definition] remains unavoidable. [To this we reply: Let it be so, provided that the property of being the objecthood delimited by a certain form (*yadrūpāvacchinnaviṣayitātva*), which is delimited by a certain relation (*yatsambandhāvacchinna*), is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of such an absence.

This is because it is intended as a qualification of the cognition that it be devoid of a subject-object content delimited by that form and delimited by a relation delimited by its connection [with the locus]; and since the aforementioned cognition possesses a subject-object content delimited by non-existence-in-general (abhāvatva) as delimited by a relation of inherence (samavāya), it is possible to exclude it. Nor does this fail even in cases where a lake or the like is the subject (pakṣa) in its specific individuality (*tattadvyaktitvena*).
In that case, it must be stated that it is impossible to exclude the obstructive cognition by making it apprehend that specific individuality (*tadvyaktitva*) as a non-existence (*abhāvatva*);
for it is impossible for that specific individuality, being distinct from a universal (*jāti*), to appear [in cognition] in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*).

Since its status as the delimiting condition (*pakṣatāvacchedakatā*) of the subject must be stated precisely as "the exclusion from that individual and others," a cognition apprehending that specific individuality as being an absence (*abhāvatva*) does not have as its object that which is delimited by the [required] form. And if, for fear of infinite regress, that specific individuality [is not admitted];
If it is considered that one must necessarily accept that even what is distinct from the universal (jāti) appears by its own nature, as there is no other alternative,
then [the relation] is by way of both relations: being qualified by the objectivity (viṣayatā) determined by itself, and being different from itself.

The property of being the delimitor of the counterpositiveness of such an absence— which is the property of being the objectness delimited by a certain form (Y) as qualified by the objectness delimited by another form (X)— should be qualified by the objectness delimited by that [other] form (X), insofar as it belongs to a cognition that is devoid of the objectness delimited by that [first] form (Y) as qualified by the objectness delimited by that [other] form (X).
This is the delimiting factor of the definition.

It should be understood that the exclusion of the cognition "the absence-possessor possesses the absence of fire-exclusion" (vahnibhāvavān vahnibhāvābhāvavān) occurs precisely because [the subject] does not possess a qualificative state delimited by absence-ness (abhāvatva) as determined by a qualificand-state determined by a qualificative state delimited by fire-exclusion-ness (vahnibhāvatva).

This is because there is no qualificative state delimited by absence-ness of its own nature (svātmakābhāvatva) as determined by a qualificand-state determined by a qualificative state delimited by fire-exclusion-ness.

Even in the cognition "the lake possesses water other than [water]," it is necessary to include the condition of being "distinct from itself" (*svabhinnatva*) in order to justify that the property of being the objecthood delimited by that form (*tadrūpāvacchinnaviṣayatātva*), as qualified by the objecthood delimited by that same form, serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absence [of the probans]. This should be understood with great care. Although, this being the case, the pursuit of the condition of "not occurring in anything else" (*anatiriktavṛttitva*) would be fruitless.

Since it is possible to exclude erroneous cognition (*bhrama*) simply by [defining the object as] possessing a qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā*) delimited by conjunction (*saṃyogatva*), which is itself determined by a relational objectness (*saṃsargaviṣayatā*) determined by a modehood (*prakāratā*) delimited by being a relation (*saṃsargatva*), the stated purpose [of the definition] is untenable.

Nevertheless, even a cognition such as "the mountain is stony" occurring at the time of the cognition "the mountain is not fiery" acts as an obstacle to inference by way of being a perception of a property that delimits [the absence of the probandum].

There would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a stone mountain regarding that object; however, if the definition is restricted to "subsisting in no more than [the locus]," there is no over-extension, because such a cognition at a time when one lacks the cognition "this is not a stone mountain" does not act as an impediment (*apratibandhakatva*).
"Resting upon such a certainty": thus, in the phrase "of knowledge" (*jñānasya*), the meaning of the genitive case is "resting upon" (*niṣṭhatva*);

this [meaning] is then construed with "having as its object" (*yad-viṣayakatve*). Consequently, even though the property of having as its object a mountain that lacks fire is not co-extensive with the obstructor-ness (*pratibandhakatā*) of inference, [the definition still holds].

The point is that there is no impossibility [of the definition] because that [determinant], as qualified by the property of occurring in such a certainty, does not occur beyond [the set of obstructors].
Although the property of having as its object a mountain possessing the absence of fire—
which serves as the qualificand— occurs beyond the state of being an obstructor, it nonetheless does not occur beyond [the set of obstructors] even when that [absence] is qualified [by the mountain].
This is difficult to maintain, because since the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) is not distinct from the pure (*śuddha*),

one must admit that even in the case of "existence qualified by being other than a quality" (*guṇānyatva-viśiṣṭa-sattā*), it resides in a quality. Furthermore, it is not the case that the property-ness delimited by some form (*yadrūpāvacchinna*) which qualifies the subjectivity residing in such a certainty is a non-delimiter of the locus of the absence of the obstructiveness to inference.

It must be stated that [the term] is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣaṇīya*). Since the nature of being the object-ness of such a qualified [cognition] (*tādṛśaviśiṣṭaviṣayitātva*) consists of both [the nature of being the object-ness of the qualifier and the nature of being the object-ness of the qualified], it is impossible to establish that neither of these two is a delimitor of the locus-ness (*vṛttitāvacchedaka*) in a locus where each is devoid of the capacity to obstruct (*pratibandhakatāśūnya*), because [if they were so,] the locus-ness in both would not be delimited by either of them. Nevertheless, non-redundant locus-ness (*anatiriktavṛtitva*) is simply the state of having that [property] as its pervader (*svavyāpaka-tatkatva*); and thus...

The meaning culminates in this: a defect (*doṣa*) is that which is delimited by a specific form (*tadrūpāvacchinna*) such that the state of being an obstacle to inference (*anumitipratibandhakatva*) pervades the objectivity (*viṣayitā*) qualified by the occurrence of such a certainty (*tādṛśaniścayavṛttitvaviśiṣṭa*). Furthermore, since the locus of the qualified (*viśiṣṭādhikaraṇatā*) is included within the body of this pervasion (*vyāpakatā*), there is no room for the aforementioned defect.

Alternatively, it should be understood that what is intended is the absence of the state of being a counter-argument (pratibandhakatā) in the locus of the property of being the objecthood delimited by a certain form qualified by the occurrence of such a certainty.
Here, this should be noted: [the definition fails] in the case of that which is composed of the state of possessing the absence of fire, as delimited by the property of possessing water.

Because [the pseudo-reason] "possessing a nature other than that which exists" (*anyabhāvavat*), "like water" (*jalavat*), or "like a lake containing water" (*vṛtajalavad-hrada*) is not included within the subverters (*bādhaka*) and so forth, it lacks the status of a valid locus (*lakṣya*). Consequently, since its objective content (*viṣayitā*) occurs as no more than a counter-impediment to inference by way of being the perceived delimiting property (*avacchedaka-dharma*), there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case. Nor can it be argued that [this is avoided] because it is the delimitor of the counter-impediment to the apprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*pakṣa*).
Nor should it be argued that, because it is distinct from *satpratipakṣa* (the counter-balanced reason), subsumption under *bādha* (sublation) alone should be accepted;

for if that were the case, then since whatever fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) exists in a particular instance would have its pervader (*tadvyāpya*) subsumed under that very same category, there would be the undesirable consequence of deficiency (*nyūnatā*) due to the failure to state the subsumption of even its delimiting factor (*tadavacchedaka*).

Therefore, one must accept that the author’s intended meaning is precisely this: that the status of being a sublater (*pratibandhakatā*) by way of the perception of a delimiting property (*avacchedaka-dharma*) does not constitute a component of the definition of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Nor [is it the case] by virtue of [the sublativeness] not being delimited by the qualification of a cognition (*jñāna-vaiśiṣṭya*).

The nature of the obstructor (pratibandhakatā) must be specified; since the cognition of the delimiting property (avacchedakadharmadarśana) is an obstructor only as a cognition qualified by another cognition, the nature of the obstructor must be specified as being unconditioned by the qualification of that [other] cognition.

It should not be argued that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭa*). For if that were the case, even at the time of the two cognitions— "the absence of fire is pervasive in water" and "the lake possesses water"— there would be no production of the inference "the lake possesses fire."

For even the cognition whose object is the counter-positive of existence must be stated to have the status of an obstructor precisely as a cognition qualified by another cognition; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in that case.
